problem_text: In the pattern avoidance game $PAG(n, P)$, what is $W(n, P)$ when $n$ is even and $P$ consists of an odd number of identical rows or an odd number of identical columns?

posts.title: pattern avoidance game
posts.text:
[quote=][quote=]Generalizing for $k$ and $n\geq k$, $W (n,P) $ should be Player $\left[(k-1)n+1 \mod 2\right] + 1$. This follows from $ex (n,P)=n (k-1) $ since there are n rows, and you can only fill each with k-1 entries.  If $n (k-1) $ is odd, Player 1 wins.  If it is even, Player 2 wins.[/quote]

This is right, any ideas for how to extend this result to other patterns?

For example, what if $P$ is a $j \times k$ matrix with all entries equal to $1$?
If $n$ is even and $j$ or $k$ is odd, is there an easy way to determine $W(n, P)$?
What if $n$ is odd, or $j$ and $k$ are both even?[/quote]

Does anyone see a way to prove that $W(n, P) = 2$ for certain $n$ and $P$ by showing that Player $2$ can mimic Player $1$'s moves without causing the matrix to contain $P$?

posts.title: pattern avoidance game
posts.text:
If $n$ is even and at least one of $j$ and $k$ is odd, player 2 wins. Say $k$ is odd, then after player 1 flips $(i, 2d+1)$, player 2 flips $(i, 2d+2)$, or vice versa. So after each move of player 2 column $2d+1$ and $2d+2$ are identical for all $d$, and the matrix cannot start to contain $P$ which has an odd number of identical columns after player 2's move.

So, to generalize: if $n$ is even and $P$ is composed of an odd number of identical rows or columns, $W(n, P)=2$.

That's a nice generalization. Is there a way to characterize all of the matrices $P$ for which Player $2$ can guarantee victory with this strategy when $n$ is even? Are there matrices for which Player $1$ can guarantee victory when Player $2$ uses this same strategy against them?

posts.title: pattern avoidance game
posts.text:
It depends on what exactly "this strategy" is, in particular the way of mimic employed by player 2 :) If player 2 always flips $(i, 2d+1)$ after player 1 flips $(i, 2d+2)$ and vice versa, then a pattern $P$ with even number of columns, along with column 1 identical to column 2, column 3 to column 4, etc.  guarantees victory for player 1.

As for all the matrices $P$ for which player 2 can guarantee victory with this strategy when $n$ is even, I haven't got better idea than those with odd number of identical rows or columns.

I also wonder for an odd $n$, suppose the center of $n$-by-$n$ matrix has coordinate $(0, 0)$. What patterns lead to player 1���s victory if they first flip $(0, 0)$ and then flips $(-i, -j)$ after player 2 flips $(i, j)$.

Actually, it looks like Player $2$ can win if Player $1$ uses the $(i, j) \rightarrow (-i,-j)$ strategy on a $k \times k$ identity matrix for $k \neq 2$, but Player $1$ wins when $k = 2$. The same is true for reflections of $k \times k$ identity matrices. Can anyone confirm or refute this?

posts.title: pattern avoidance game
posts.text: Yes, if $n=k$ player 2 can flip along the main diagonal. Otherwise when $n>k$, player 2 can flip $(2-t,t-1),(3-t,t-2),\ldots,(k-1-t,-k+2+t)$ sequentially, and then flip the upper left corner to win, where $t=\lfloor k/2\rfloor$. I haven't carefully checked the boundary condition though.

problem_text: In the pattern avoidance game $PAG(n, P)$, what is $W(n, P)$ when $P$ is the $2 \times 2$ identity matrix?

posts.title: pattern avoidance game
posts.text: If $P$ is a $2$-by-$2$ identity matrix, player 1 wins. He/She first flips the top left corner, and then both players are left with only column $1$ and row $1$ to flip in order not to contain $P$. The total number of $0$ left in column $1$ and row $1$ is $2(n-1)$, an even number.

problem_text: In the $d$-player pattern avoidance game on an $n \times n$ matrix where $L_d(n,P)$ denotes the losing player, does $L_d(n,P) \equiv L_{md}(n,P) \pmod{d}$ hold for all $n, m, d$ when $P$ is a $k \times 1$ all-ones pattern?

posts.title: pattern avoidance game
posts.text:
A simple thought. All player indices below are $0$-based.

For an even $k$, we should have loser $L_2(n,P)\equiv L_k(n,P)\mod 2$, where the subscript means the number of players. This is because if $L_2(n,P)=1$, then player $0, 2, 4, \ldots, k-2$ can collectively deploy player $0$'s winning strategy as if there are only $2$ players to make sure not to lose. Similar argument goes for if $L_2(n,P)=0$.

To generalize, $L_d(n,P)\equiv L_{md}(n,P)\mod d$.

Similar argument goes for if $L_2(n,P)=0$.

To generalize, $L_d(n,P)\equiv L_{md}(n,P)\mod d$.[/quote]

Given this result, say that $M$ is a product of positive integers $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{k}$ that are pairwise coprime. Can we determine $L_{M}(n, P)$ if we know $L_{m_{i}}(n, P)$ for each $1 \leq i \leq k$?

posts.title: pattern avoidance game
posts.text: This is an interesting generalization! Yes, because of Chinese remainder theorem, $L_M(n,P)$ can be uniquely determined based on $L_{m_1}(n,P), \ldots, L_{m_k}(n,P)$. The computation is exactly as described in the Theorem, by $L_M(n,P)\equiv \sum_{i=1}^kL_{m_i}(n,P)\frac{M}{m_i}[(\frac{M}{m_i})^{-1}]_{m_i}\pmod M$, where $[a^{-1}]_b$ is the multiplicative inverse of $a\pmod b$.

posts.title: pattern avoidance game
posts.text: It turns out that for $k\times 1$ pattern $P$, $L_d(n,P)\equiv L_{md}(n,P)\mod d$ for all $n, m, d$, because there's no strategy in this case other than not to flip a $k$-th one in any column.

problem_text: What is $ex2(w_1, \ldots, w_d, P)$, the maximum number of ones in a $w_1 \times \cdots \times w_d$ zero-one matrix that avoids the $d$-dimensional $2 \times \cdots \times 2$ identity matrix $P$?

posts.title: pattern avoidance game
posts.text:
I doubt the result below is already known.

Interestingly, as a side product if we generalize to start with an $h\times w$ zero matrix, then $L_d(h, w, P)=(w+h-1)\mod d$ if $P$ is $2\times 2$ identity matrix. Player index is 0-based.

To see this, first define a maximal $h\times w$ matrix as a matrix that avoids $P$ and will contain $P$ if any of its zero is flipped to one. We claim that all maximal matrices have $w+h-1$ ones. Now let $A$ be a maximal matrix.

Every column of $A$ has at least an one entry. To see this, take any entry $A_{i,j}$, there cannot be an one entry both to its upper left and lower right direction.  If there's an one to its upper left, decrease $i$ until there isn't -- now there's an one to its left, and none to its lower right, so $A_{i,j}$ should be one.

For $1\leq i\leq w$, define $h_i$ as the smallest row index such that $A_{h_i,i}=1$. The process above shows that $\{h_i\}$ is a non-increasing sequence.  Moreover, for each column $i>1$ there's no reason any of $A_{h_i,i}, A_{h_i+1,i},\ldots,A_{h_{i-1},i}$ is not one. Similarly $A_{h_1,1},\ldots,A_{h,1}$ should all be one. So each column of $A$ has consecutive ones overlapping with its previous column at exactly one position.  The total number of ones is thus $w+h-1$.

posts.title: pattern avoidance game
posts.text:
[quote=]I doubt the result below is already known.

Interestingly, as a side product if we generalize to start with an $h\times w$ zero matrix, then $L_d(h, w, P)=(w+h-1)\mod d$ if $P$ is $2\times 2$ identity matrix. Player index is 0-based.
[/quote]
Turns out this can generalize to $d$-dimensional identity matrix.

From now on $P$ is defined as $2\times\ldots\times 2$ $d$-dimensional identity
matrix. \\


For notational simplicty we define {\it 2-contain} same as {\it contain}, except
when $d=1$ a matrix {\it 2-contains} $P$ as long as it has multiple one entries.
Likewise {\it 2-avoid} and $ex2$ follows naturally from {\it 2-contain} thus
defined.\\


Define $ex2(w_1,\ldots,w_d,P)$ the maximum number of one entries in
any $w_1\times\ldots\times w_d$ matrix that 2-avoids $P$.\\

Theorem: $ex2(w_1,\ldots,w_d,P)=\prod_{i=1}^dw_i-\prod_{i=1}^d(w_i-1)$. Moreover, every
maximal $w_1\times\ldots\times w_d$ matrix that 2-avoids $P$ has exactly
$ex2(w_1,\ldots,w_d,P)$ one entries. A maximal matrix is one such that flipping
any zero to one makes it 2-contain $P$.\\

The theorem is trivial when $d=1$ or when $w_i=1$ for some $i$ in $[1,d]$.\\

Let $M$ be a maximal $w_1\times\ldots\times w_d$ matrix that 2-avoids $P$. We
focus on the $d$-rows of $M$.


A $d$-row $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{d-1})$ is a {\it ancestor} of $d$-row
$y=(y_1,\ldots,y_{d-1})$ if $x_i<y_i$ for $1\leq i\leq d-1$. We say $y$ is
a {\it descendant} of $x$. $A(x)$ and $D(x)$ are the sets of ancestors and
descendants of $x$, respectively. Define $M(x,x_d)=M_{x_1,\ldots,x_d}$.
Ancestor and descendant relations are transitive, and the graphs of these two
relations are directed acyclic.\\

Lemma 1: Every $d$-row of $M$ has some one entry.

Proof: Given a $d$-row $x$, if $A(x)$ is empty, then $M(x,w_d)=1$. If $D(x)$ is
empty, then $M(x,1)=1$. If both sets are not empty, $l(A(x))$, the smallest $d$-coordinate
of one entries in $A(x)$ must be greater than or equal to $h(D(x))$, the largest
$d$-coordinate of one entries in $D(x)$, otherwise $M$ 2-contains $P$. Then pick
some $y$ in $[h(D(x)), l(A(x))]$ and having $M(x,y)=1$ doesn't make $M$
2-contain $P$.\\

Lemma 2: Given any $d$-row $x$, the set $\{y:M(x,y)=1\}$ forms an integer
arithmetic progressive sequence with common difference 1.

Proof: If $M(x,y_1)=M(x,y_2)=1$ for $y_1\leq y_2$, then setting any $y$ in
$[y_1,y_2]$ doesn't make $M$ 2-contain $P$.\\

For a $d$-row $x$ define $l(x)$ and $h(x)$ as the minimum and maximum $y$ such that
$M(x,y)=1$, respectively. $w(M)$, the number of one entries in $M$, is then
$\sum_{x}h(x)-l(x)+1$.\\

Lemma 3: $h(x)=\min(w_d, \min_{z\in A(x)}l(z))$

Proof: If $h(x)>l(z)$ for some $z\in A(x)$, then $M$ 2-contains $P$. On the
other hand, if $h(x)<\min_{z\in A(x)}l(z)$, setting $M(x,\min_{z\in
A(x)}l(z))=1$ doesn't make $M$ 2-contain $P$.\\

Lemma 4: $l(x)=\max(1, \max_{z\in D(x)}h(z))$

Proof: If $l(x)<h(z)$ for some $z\in D(x)$, then $M$ 2-contains $P$. On the
other hand, if $l(x)>\max_{z\in D(x)}h(z)$, setting $M(x,\max_{z\in
D(x)}h(z))=1$ doesn't make $M$ 2-contain $P$.\\

We're now going to prove the theorem by mathematical reduction on $d$ and
$w_d$ through the following lemmas. Assume the theorem holds with
$1,2,\ldots,d-1$ dimensions, and for
$(w_1,\ldots,w_{d-1},1),(w_1,\ldots,w_{d-1},2),\ldots,(w_1,\ldots,w_{d-1},w_d-1)$.

Lemma 5: A matrix $M$ 2-avoiding $P$ is maximal if
$h(x)$ and $l(x)$ satisfies equations in Lemma 3 and Lemma 4 for every $d$-row $x$.\\
Proof: Clearly, if there's an one entry in some $d$-row $x$ with $d$-coordinate
$y$
bigger than $\min(w_d, \min_{z\in A(x)}l(z))$, then $y$ either goes
beyond $w_d$, which is impossible, or $y>l(z)$ for some ancestor $z$ of $x$, and $M$ 2-contains
$P$. Similarly we couldn't have any one entry in any $d$-row $x$ with
$d$-coordinate less than $\max(1, \max_{z\in D(x)}h(z))$.\\

We say that a $d$-row $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{d-1})$ is a {\it semi-ancestor} of $d$-row
$y=(y_1,\ldots,y_{d-1})$ if $x_i\leq y_i$ for all $i$ in $[1,d-1]$ and $x_i<y_i$
for some $i$ in $[1,d-1]$.\\

Lemma 6: If the set $\{x:h(x)=w_d, A(x)\neq\emptyset\}\neq\emptyset$, there
are $d$-rows $x$ and $x'$, such that $x=(x'_1+1,\ldots,x'_{d-1}+1)$,
$h(x)=w_d>l(x)$, and $x'$ has no other descendant $z$ with $h(z)=w_d$.

Proof: In the first stage we find a $d$-row $x$ with $h(x)=w_d>l(x)$ and
$A(x)\neq\emptyset$. Starting
from any $d$-row $x$ with $h(x)=w_d$, if $l(x)=w_d$, then there is descendant $z$ of $x$
with $h(z)=w_d$. We move from $x$ to $z$ and see if $l(z)<w_d$. We repeat the
process until we find a $x''$ with $h(x'')=w_d>l(x'')$, which is guaranteed to have
non-empty ancestor set $A(x'')$. Such $x''$ exists because there are only finite
number of $d$-rows, and whenever we hit one without descendants,
$l(x'')=1$. We set $x=x''$ and $x'=(x_1-1,\ldots,x_{d-1}-1)$.

In the second stage, if $x'$ has no other descendant $z$ with $h(z)=w_d$ then we're done. If it does,
$D(z)\subset D(x)$ so $l(z)\leq l(x)<w_d$, i.e. $z$ qualifies the requirement
for $x$ too. Moreover $x$ is a semi-ancestor of $z$, so we reset $x$ to $z$ and $x'=(x_1-1,\ldots,x_{d-1}-1)$. We repeat
this process again and again until $x'$ has no other descendant $z$ with
$h(z)=w_d$. This process terminates because in the sequence of $x$ we found, each
element is a semi-ancestor of it subsequent element, and this sequence couldn't
be infinitely long.\\


Lemma 7: If the set $\{x:h(x)=w_d, A(x)\neq\emptyset\}\neq\emptyset$, we can
convert $M$ to another maximal matrix $M'$ that 2-avoids $P$ with the set smaller and yet
$w(M)=w(M')$.

Proof: We find
$d$-rows $x$ and $x'$, such that $x=(x'_1+1,\ldots,x'_{d-1}+1)$,
$h(x)=w_d>l(x)$, and $x'$ has no other descendant $z$ with $h(z)=w_d$.
Construct $M'$
identical to $M$ except $h'(x)=w_d-1$ and $l'(x')=w_d-1$. $M'$ has fewer
$d$-rows in the set $\{x:h'(x)=w_d, A(x)\neq\emptyset\}$, plus
$w(M')=w(M)$.

We now show that $M'$ is still a maximal matrix that 2-avoids $P$. The only
changes we make are to decrease $h(x)$ and $l(x')$ by 1. Clearly equation in
Lemma 3 is
not violated by $M'$, because $x'$ is an ancester of $x$. The only possibility
that $M'$ violates equation in Lemma 4 is that $x'$ has another descendant $z$ with
$h(z)=w_d$. But this is impossible because of the choice we make with $x'$, so
we're done.\\

Lemma 8: If $\{x:h(x)=w_d,A(x)\neq\emptyset\}=\emptyset$, then
$w(M)=\prod_{i=1}^dw_i-\prod_{i=1}^d(w_i-1)$.

Proof: Transform $M$ to $M'$ by removing the $w_d$-th $d$-cross section. Then
since $h(x)=w_d$ if $A(x)=\emptyset$,

$$
w(M')=w(M)-|\{x:A(x)=\emptyset\}|
$$

By assumption
$$w(M')=w_1\times\ldots\times
w_{d-1}(w_d-1)-(w_1-1)\times\ldots\times (w_{d-1}-1)(w_d-2)$$

$A(x)=\emptyset$ if and only if at least one of the coordinates
$x_1,\ldots,x_{d-1}$ is 1. So
$$
|\{x:A(x)=\emptyset\}|=w_1\times\ldots\times w_{d-1}-(w_1-1)\times\ldots\times
(w_{d-1}-1)
$$
Adding them together,
$$
w(M)=\prod_{i=1}^dw_i-\prod_{i=1}^d(w_i-1)
$$

Finally, given any matrix $M$ that maximally 2-avoids $P$, if necessary by
applying Lemma 7 a finite number of times we can 
convert it to another maximal $M'$ with the same number of one entries, still
2-avoids $P$, and with empty $\{x:h(x)=w_d,A(x)\neq\emptyset\}$. And then by
Lemma 8 we have 
$w(M)=\prod_{i=1}^dw_i-\prod_{i=1}^d(w_i-1)$. This concludes our proof.

[quote=]To clarify, each player can choose one or multiple 0s to flip to 1, right?[/quote]

Each turn, the player changes a single 0 to a 1. If the players were allowed to change multiple 0s to 1s on each turn, then the first player would always win, except when $P$ is the $1 \times 1$ identity matrix, or if every entry in $P$ is 0.

posts.text: What is an optimal strategy?

posts.title: pattern avoidance game
posts.text:
[quote=]What is an optimal strategy?[/quote]

Here is what we mean by an optimal strategy for this game: If either player can make a move that will eventually force the other player to lose (possibly after both players have made additional moves), then the player will make such a move. Moreover, the players will also avoid moves that will eventually cause themselves to lose, unless there is no other choice for the move.

posts.title: pattern avoidance game
posts.text:
The comments I will make below are all referencing part (a) of the problem: 

[b]Lemma[/b]: If \(n \ge 1\) and \(k = 1\), then the \(W(n, P)\) will always be Player 2. 
[b]Proof [/b]: Let \(A\) be a \(n \times n\) all zeroes matrix: \(\left[ \begin{matrix} 0 & 0 & \cdots  \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots  \\ \vdots  & \vdots  & \ddots  \end{matrix} \right] \). 
Let \(P\) be a \(1 \times 1\) all ones matrix: \([1]\). Now, the game is defined such that a player must change one and only one zero in \(A\) and if the resulting matrix \(A'\) contains the forbidden pattern \(P\), that player is out. If Player 1 turns any zero in \(A\) to a one, it will contain the forbidden pattern \(P\). Thus Player 1 is the loser while \(W(n, P)\) is Player 2.

posts.title: pattern avoidance game
posts.text:
This is still referencing part (a) of the problem: 

[b]Lemma[/b]: If \(n = 2\) and \(k = 2\), then the \(W(n, P)\) will always be Player 2. 
[b]Proof[/b]: Let \(A\) be a \(2 \times 2\) all zeroes matrix: \(\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). 
Let \(P\) be a \(2 \times 1\) all ones matrix: \(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\1 \end{bmatrix}\). 
First, Player 1 has to change one of the zeroes in \(A\) to one. It does not matter which one he changes, so I will say that he changed the top left zero to a one: \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). 
Next Player 2 has to take his turn. Player 2 cannot change the bottom left zero to a one; Player 2 can only change either the top right zero or the bottom right zero. I will show you both scenarios. First, however, we will say that Player two changed the top right zero to a one: \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). 
In this scenario, the \(W(n, P)\) will be Player 2 because no matter which zero Player 1 changes, the new matrix \(A'\) will always contain \(P\). 
Now, suppose that Player 2 changed the bottom right zero to a one: \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). 
In this case, the \(W(n, P)\) will still be Player 2 because no matter what Player 1 does, it will always contain the forbidden pattern \(P\).

posts.title: pattern avoidance game
posts.text: Generalizing for $k$ and $n\geq k$, $W (n,P) $ should be Player $\left[(k-1)n+1 \mod 2\right] + 1$. This follows from $ex (n,P)=n (k-1) $ since there are n rows, and you can only fill each with k-1 entries.  If $n (k-1) $ is odd, Player 1 wins.  If it is even, Player 2 wins.

problem_text: What is the time complexity of deciding whether an $h_A \times w_A$ zero-one matrix $A$ contains an $h_B \times w_B$ zero-one matrix $B$?

posts.title: Creating A Research Game
posts.text:
This is the most efficient algorithm I can think of at present for arbitrary matrices $A$ and $B$:
[code]
1. Create a set of all transformations of A, call it X.
2. Create a set of all transformations of B, call it Y.
3.Cross check, is there any coinciding elements.
4. If there are, A contains B.
5. Else, A does not contain B.
[/code]
 

This is probably the brute force algorithm that was mentioned above. But if there isn't a pattern, I think this is the best way.

posts.title: Creating A Research Game
posts.text:
If I am correct, we can do brute with code pretty easily.  Pseudocode:

[code]
A = an array with elements of Matrix A
B = an array with elements of Matrix B

flag = True

for elements of B:
    if not current element in A:
        flag = False

if flag:
    print "A contains B"

[/code]

For small $A$ and $B$, I don't think this wouldn't be horribly inefficient, although this method is admittedly rough.

This algorithm would not work for checking containment. For example, let A be the $2 \times 1$ matrix with all ones and let B be the $1 \times 2$ matrix with all ones. Then the sets X and Y would both contain the elements A and B, but A does not contain B.

This would not work for checking containment, but you can modify it to make it work. Instead of defining A to be an array with elements of matrix A, define A to be a set with all patterns contained in A. 

All of the patterns contained in A can be obtained by selecting a submatrix of A and changing some number of ones (possibly none) in the submatrix to zeroes. The resulting modified submatrix of A is a pattern, so you can build the set of patterns contained in A by iterating through all of the submatrices of A. If the current submatrix has k ones, then it contributes at most $2^{k}$ patterns to the set.

posts.title: Creating A Research Game
posts.text:
If $B$ is a $k\times k$ identity matrix. The following algorithm takes $O(w_A\times h_A)$ time.

It maintains an array $D[h_A][w_A]$. For $1\leq r\leq h_A$, $D[r][c]$ is the
maximum number of ones from column $c$ to the last column of $A$ such that (1)
all these ones are in rows between $r$ and $h_A$, inclusive.  (2) all these ones
form a $D[r][c]\times D[r][c]$ identity matrix when we remove all columns and rows not containing these ones.

Initially $D[r][c]$ is 0 for all $r$. The algorithm updates $D$ as follows.

For $c$ = $w_A$ to $1$
..For $r$ = $h_A$ to $1$
....$D[r][c]=\max(D[r+1][c],D[r][c+1])$
....if $A(r,c) = 1$
......$D[r][c]=\max(D[r][c], 1 + D[r+1][c+1])$

The algorithm reports $A$ contains $B$ whenever some $D[r][c]$ hits $k$. Replace
any $D$ above with index out of bound by value $0$. There's technique to reduce to using
only 2 1-D arrays rather than a 2-D array. Let me know if I got anything wrong.

problem_text: What is the time complexity of deciding whether an $h_A \times w_A$ zero-one matrix $A$ contains the $j$-column-identity matrix (the $k \times k$ identity matrix with each 1 replaced by a $j \times 1$ all-ones column)?

posts.title: Creating A Research Game
posts.text:
For matrix $B$ obtained by replacing each one of an identity matrix with a $j\times 1$ matrix with all ones -- let's denote it by $j$-column-identity matrix -- I think the following variation works and still takes $O(h_A\times w_A)$. Please let me know if it doesn't.

$D[r][c]$ now indicates the maximum width of $j$-column-identity matrix contained by the submatrix of $A$ within row $r$ to $h_A$ and column $c$ to $w_A$. The algorithm reports $true$ if any $D[r][c]$ reaches $k$.

The algorithm proceeds as before, but for each column $c$ and each row $r$, it needs to know a number $r+j\leq H(r,c)\leq h_A$ first. $H(r,c)$ is as small as possible such that in column $c$ the number of $1$s between row $r$ and $H(r,c)-1$, inclusive, is at least $j$. If in column $c$ there are less than $j$ $1$s from row $r$ through the bottom we can set $H(r,c)=\infty$. Since the outer loop of the algorithm scans each column and the inner loop scans each row, simple technique ensures the overhead of computing $H(r,c)$ is $O(h_A)$ per column, and hence doesn't impact overall asymptotic complexity.

So the recurrence becomes

$D[r][c]=\max(D[r+1][c],D[r][c+1])$
If $A[r][c]=1$
..$D[r][c]=\max(D[r][c],1+D[H(r,c)][c+1])$

posts.text: Sorry I totally missed your original post. Yes an algorithm in time $O(w^2h)$ and memory $O(w^2)$ can decide whether a given matrix $A$ contains $P$ if $P$ is $k\times 2$. It goes by keeping ${w \choose 2}$ counters and scanning row by row of $A$. In each row $i$ if both $A_{i,a}$ and $A_{i,b}$ are $1$ then counter $(a,b)$ is incremented by $1$. So, for patterns $P_{m\times n}=L(m,n)$, defined as L-shaped $1$s with $P_{i,j}=1$ iff $j=1$ or $i=m$, we know $ex(n,P)=O(n)$. And the $O(hw)$ algorithm to determine if $A$ contains $P$ is this. 0 & \ldots & 0 & 1 & 0 & \ldots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
0 & \ldots & 0 & 1 & 0 & \ldots & 0 \\
1 & \ldots & 1 & 1 & 1 & \ldots &1\\
\end{pmatrix}$, $ex(n,P)=O(n)$ and a similar $O(wh)$ algorithm can find out whether $A$ contains $P$.

problem_text: Given an $h_A \times w_A$ zero-one matrix $A$ with $x$ ones (represented as a doubly linked structure with 4 directional pointers per node: next/prev in row and next/prev in column), what is the time complexity of deciding whether $A$ contains the cross pattern $P_{a \times b}$ (where $P_{i,j} = 1$ iff $i = c$ or $j = d$)?

posts.title: Creating A Research Game
posts.text:
[quote=]This shows that given an $O(wh)$ algorithm to determine whether a $w \times h$ matrix contains $P$, there is an $O(x^2)$ algorithm to determine whether x ones contain $P$. For $k \times 1$ matrices $P$ with all ones, is there an $O(x)$ algorithm?

Are there other patterns with an $O(x)$ algorithm?[/quote]

I was working on 'cross' pattern $P_{a\times b}$, with $P(i,j)=1$ iff $i=c$ or $j=d$ where $c$ and $d$ are constants such that $1\leq c\leq a$ and $1\leq d\leq b$.

It turns out to also depend on the format the list of ones are given in this particular example. I found $O(x)$ algorithm exists if the ones are in the following format. Each one is associated with a distinct node, which has at most 4 links (pointers) to other nodes.

One link to the next one to the right in the same row, or if it doesn't exist, the left most one in the next row below
One to the next one to the left in the same row, or if it doesn't exist, the right most one in the next row below
...and something similar for vertical links.

Each node may have special marks indicating it's the top/bottom/right most/left most one of that column/row.

Following these 4 links and marks, we can compute and store $R(node)$, the number of ones to its right in the same row, and similary $L(node),U(node),D(node)$, in 4 linear traversals, i.e. $O(x)$ time. Finally, in one extra traversal the algorithm reports $true$ if a node's $L$, $R$, $D$, and $U$ values are all above respective thresholds.

problem_text: Given $x$ ones in a $d$-dimensional zero-one array (represented as a list of lists of linked lists, where the top level indexes dimension and direction, the second level indexes rows/columns, and each linked list holds the ones in that row/column), what is the time complexity of deciding whether the array contains the $d$-dimensional cross pattern $P$ (where $P$ has a $1$ at position $(i_1, \ldots, i_d)$ iff $i_j = c_j$ for some fixed $j$ and constant $c_j$)?

posts.title: Creating A Research Game
posts.text:
I think the answer is positive. The assumed input data structure and the needed algorithm could be generalized to $d$-dimensional case. Each node has $2d$ pointers pointing to its $2d$ neighbors (actually $d$ pointers work too, just need extra $O(x)$ backtrack time and $O(x)$ memory for backtracking), and $2d$ counters storing the number of ones beyond itself in each direction. The overall $2d+1$ $O(x)$ time traversal could be reduced to $2d$, because in the last traversal when the last counter is populated, we can check if all counters are above the thresholds.

In the previous post I mentioned the pointer has to point to, for example, the top ones in the next column if the current node is the bottom one in its column. This somewhat weird requirement can be avoided. The only reason for this requirement was to enable a smooth traversal. To get rid of it, in each dimension and each direction we can require the node be presented as a list of linked lists, one for each row or column in the 2-D case. And the traversal for all ones in each dimension and direction is then accomplished by traversing each linked list in the list. Therefore, the final data structure is a list of lists of linked lists :) Each element in the highest level list corresponds to a dimension and a direction, each element in the second level list is a linked list corresponding to, for example, a column in the 2-D case.

problem_text: For a separated minimally non-linear bipartite ordered graph with $k$ total vertices, what are upper and lower bounds on $|E(G)|$?

posts.title: minimally non-linear sequences and 0-1 matrices
posts.text:
See my thoughts inline.

[quote=]

Here are a few more questions related to these results:

What is an upper bound on the number of edges in any separated minimally non-linear bipartite ordered graph that has $k$ total vertices (including the vertices in both parts)?
[/quote]

Let the first and second part has $w$ and $h$ vertices, i.e. $w+h=k$. $|E(G)|$ is bounded by $2h+w$ and $2w+h$. So $|E(G)| \leq k+\min(w,h)\leq 3k/2$.

[quote=]
What is a lower bound on the number of edges in any separated minimally non-linear bipartite ordered graph that has $k$ total vertices (including the vertices in both parts)?
[/quote]
$|E(G)|\geq\max(w,h)\geq k/2$.
[quote=]
What is a lower bound on the number of ones in any minimally non-linear $0-1$ matrix with $k$ rows?
[/quote]
A naive bound is $k$.

[quote=]
Is $2\sum_{i = 1}^{4k-2}(2^{k}-1)^{i}$ an upper bound on the number of separated minimally non-linear bipartite ordered graphs for which one of the parts has $k$ vertices? If so, is there a better upper bound?
[/quote]
Yes, but could be naively improved to $2\sum_{i=\lceil (k+2)/4 \rceil}^{4k-2}(2^{k}-1)^{i}$

[quote=]
Is there any relationship between the number of separated minimally non-linear bipartite ordered graphs for which one of the parts has $k$ vertices and the number of minimally non-linear $0-1$ matrices with $k$ rows?[/quote]
I think the former is no more than twice the latter.

I think it's positive: the number of ones of a minimally non-linear binary matrix with $k$ rows is $O(k)$.

We can ignore rows with a single one, because they contribute $O(k)$ ones. The
rest of the rows have multiple ones. We claim that every column has no more
than 2 ones, followed by the fact that there are at most $4k-2$ columns.

If some column has 2 ones, the only possible configuration is below or some
transformation
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & \ldots & 1 & \ldots & 1 \\
\ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots \\
1 & \ldots & 1 & \ldots & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
This is because $P$ avoids these 2 non-linear matrices
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 \\
1 & 1 
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Clearly there's no room for any other row with multiple ones, one of them
being in the same column. Let me know if I miss anything.

posts.title: minimally non-linear sequences and 0-1 matrices
posts.text:
[quote=]A minimally non-linear $0-1$ matrix with $h$ rows and $w$ columns has at most $w+h$ ones.

I found this property that I mentioned before quite useful:
After removing all rows with a single one from a minimally non-linear $0-1$ matrix no column has more than $2$ ones.

To prove the statement at the top, we keep doing the following:
1. For every one, if it is the only one in its column and row, remove that column and row.
2. Remove all columns with single a one.
3. Remove all rows with single a one.
4. Go to step 1.

The algorithm terminates in 3 situations. Say we perform step 1, 2, and 3 $a$, $b$, and $c$ times, respectively. Note that because of step 1, no operation leaves any column or row full of zeros.

Situation 1: we end up with a $d\times d$ matrix each with exactly $2$ ones.
\[
a+c+d=h,
a+b+d=w
\]
The number of ones in the original matrix is therefore $a+b+c+2d\leq 2a+b+c+2d=h+w$.

Situation 2: we end up with a $e\times 0$ matrix after step 2. An example is 
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 \\
0 & 1 \\
1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
So
\[
a+c+e=h,
a+b=w
\]
The number of ones is $a+b+c\leq w+h$.

Situation 3: we end up with a $0\times e$ matrix after step 3. An example is 
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 1  & 1\\
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Similarly the number of ones is bounded by $w+h$.[/quote]
This result is nice. Now the upper bound on the number of ones in a minimally non-linear $0-1$ matrix with $k$ rows is $5k-2$. Is $k$ the new upper bound for the number of edges in a minimally non-linear separated bipartite ordered graph with $k$ total vertices?

What is an upper bound on the number of edges in any separated minimally non-linear bipartite ordered graph that has $k$ total vertices (including the vertices in both parts)?

Let the first and second part has $w$ and $h$ vertices, i.e. $w+h=k$. $|E(G)|$ is bounded by $2h+w$ and $2w+h$. So $|E(G)| \leq k+\min(w,h)\leq 3k/2$.

$|E(G)|\geq\max(w,h)\geq k/2$.

What is a lower bound on the number of ones in any minimally non-linear $0-1$ matrix with $k$ rows?

A naive bound is $k$.

Is $2\sum_{i = 1}^{4k-2}(2^{k}-1)^{i}$ an upper bound on the number of separated minimally non-linear bipartite ordered graphs for which one of the parts has $k$ vertices? If so, is there a better upper bound?
[/quote]
Yes, but could be naively improved to $2\sum_{i=\lceil (k+2)/4 \rceil}^{4k-2}(2^{k}-1)^{i}$

I think the former is no more than twice the latter.

\]

Can that result be used to get upper bounds for the questions below?

posts.title: minimally non-linear sequences and 0-1 matrices
posts.text:
Seems positive for both questions.

For a matrix $P$ define $\{G_o(P)\}=\{g:P(g)=P\}$, i.e. the family of all bipartite ordered graphs with a unique decomposition into two independent sets equivalent to $P$. Then every element of $\{\{G_o(Q_1)\}, \{G_o(\bar{Q_1})\}, \{G_o(R)\}\}$ is non-linear in $ex_<$. 

Let $G$ be a graph described in either question 7 or 8, so $G$ avoids $\{\{G_o(Q_1)\}, \{G_o(\bar{Q_1})\}, \{G_o(R)\}\}$. Define an edge as $e=(v_i,v_j)$ where $v_i<v_j$. Remove all edges $(v_i,v_j)$ where $v_j$ is the smallest number $t$ such that $(v_i,t)\in E(G)$.  

The resulting graph $G'$ cannot have both edges $(v_i, v_k)$ and $(v_j, v_k)$ for any node $v_k$. Because if it does, then there are $v_i<v_a<v_k$ and $v_j<v_b<v_k$ such that $(v_i,v_a)$, $(v_i,v_k)$, $(v_j,v_b)$, and $(v_j,v_k)$ are all in $E(G)$, and therefore $G$ must contains some element in $\{\{G_o(Q_1)\}, \{G_o(\bar{Q_1})\}, \{G_o(R)\}\}$. Note that $v_a$ and $v_b$ may be identical. So $|E(G)|\leq 2k$.

The proof in the paper can also be modified to prove in a simpler way that the number of ones in a minimally nonlinear $h\times w$ $0-1$ matrix is bounded by $w+h$. We can delete the first one in every row, and the resulting matrix cannot have any column with multiple ones.

problem_text: What is an upper bound on the number of minimally non-linear sequences with $k$ distinct letters?

posts.title: minimally non-linear sequences and 0-1 matrices
posts.text:
[quote=]What is an upper bound on the number of minimally non-linear sequences with $k$ distinct letters?
[/quote]

Given that $a b a b a$ is a nonlinear sequence, does anyone see a way to show that the number of minimally non-linear sequences with $k$ distinct letters is at most $2^{k^{Ex(a b a b a, k)}}$?

These facts could be useful:
If $u$ is a linear sequence and $u'$ is obtained from $u$ by inserting the letter $a$ between two adjacent occurrences of $a$ in $u$, then $u'$ is linear.
$Ex(a b a b a, n)$ is the maximum possible length of a sequence with $n$ distinct letters and no adjacent same letters that avoids $a b a b a$.

Note that $Ex(a b a b a, n) \approx 2 n \alpha(n)$, where $\alpha(n)$ denotes the inverse Ackermann function.

Also, can a better bound be achieved by replacing $a b a b a$ with a set of forbidden sequences that includes $a b a b a$? It is known that $a b c a c b c$ is also minimally non-linear.

Interesting thoughts. Let me try it. First we claim that there is no immediate repetition greater than 2 in a minimally non-linear sequence. Suppose there is a minimally non-linear sequence $u$ with repetition of length 3. Remove one of the repetition and get $u'$. By definition $u'$ is linear, but then inserting the letter back still gives a linear sequence, a contradiction. 

So the number of repeated segments is bounded by $Ex(ababa, k)$ because $u$ avoids $ababa$. Each segment can be filled with one of the $k$ letters, with length $1$ or $2$. So the number of such sequences $u$ is bounded by $\sum_{i=1}^{Ex(ababa,k)}(2k)^i$. Alternatively, since $u$ is no longer than $2Ex(ababa,k)$, its cardinality doesn't exceed $\sum_{i=1}^{2Ex(ababa,k)}k^{i}$.

Seems $4k-2$ too for question 4.

Given a minimally non-linear bipartite ordered graph $G$, without loss of generality assume the first part $U$ has $k$ nodes. For each node $v_i$ in the second part $V$, we decide a node index in $U$ the same way we do for matrix: if $v_i$ has only one neighbor then pick it, otherwise pick the smallest neighbor different from what we pick for $v_{i-1}$. Now we get a sequence with $k$ distinct elements without repetition more than 2 because otherwise $G$ isn't minimal. The sequence can't be longer than $2Ex(abab,k)=4k-2$, or it would contain some element in

$\{\{G_o(\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix})\},\{G_o(\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & 1 & 0
\end{bmatrix})\}\}$, which has all elements non-linear.

problem_text: What are all minimally non-linear 0-1 matrices with 2 rows?

posts.title: minimally non-linear sequences and 0-1 matrices
posts.text:
[quote=]Is there a simple way to characterize all minimally non-linear 0-1 matrices with 2 rows?

What about 3 or more rows?[/quote]

Are these statements true?

There are only seven minimally non-linear 0-1 matrices with $2$ rows. These matrices include $\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1\\
1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}$, and reflections of the last three over a vertical line.

There are no singleton vertices in a minimally non-linear ordered graph.

Yes these should be the only minimally nonlinear $0-1$ matrices with $2$ rows.

A $h\times 2$ minimally nonlinear $0-1$ matrix $A$ has at most $h+1$ ones except for $R$. So it has $h$ or $h+1$ ones, because with less than $h$ ones some row will be empty.  

Case 1: $A$ has $h+1$ ones. Obviously there's one row with $2$ ones and the rest have $1$ one. The ones above this row must be in the same column, otherwise $A$ contains some reflection or rotation of
$\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1\\
1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}$ or
$\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 \\
0 & 1 \\
1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}$. Similary the ones below this row are in the same column.  Therefore the ones either form a L-shape or something like $\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 \\
1 & 1 \\
0 & 1 \\
0 & 1 
\end{bmatrix}$, both of which are linear.

Case 2: $A$ has $h$ ones. Apparently each row has $1$ one. Because $A$ avoids $\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 \\
0 & 1 \\
1 & 0 \\
0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}$, $A$ must be either rows with $1$ at the left followed by rows with $1$ at the right, and optionally followed by rows with $1$ at the left again. The former is linear, and the latter reduces to a row with $1$ at the left, followed $t$ row(s) with $1$ at the right, and followed by a row with $1$ at the left, which is also linear.

posts.title: minimally non-linear sequences and 0-1 matrices
posts.text:
Below are some small improvements.

A minimally nonlinear $h\times w$ $0-1$ matrix has at most $w+h-1$ ones, except for $R$. This is because after removing the left most one in each row, the first column is empty and the resulting matrix has at most $w-1$ ones. The similar applies to bipartite ordered graph, separated or not. For minimally nonlinear ordered graph with $k$ nodes, the upper bounds is now $2k-2$, because edge removal deletes at most $k-1$ edges as no edge in the form of $(v_k, v_i)$ exists with $v_k<v_i$ to be deleted, and after that there are at most $k-1$ edges since no edge in the form of $(v_i, v_1)$ exists with $v_i<v_1$.

The upper bound of the number of minimally nonlinear $h\times w$ $0-1$ matrices could be improved from $(2^h-1)^w$ to $w^h(h+1)^{w-1}$. Since the ratio of $h$ and $w$ is bounded this is asymptotically better. To show it, there are $w^h$ combinations of the deleted ones in the first stage. After that each column except the first has at most an one, giving $(h+1)^{w-1}$. The similar should replace all occurrences of $(2^i-1)^k$.

When we prove a statement about some minimally nonlinear matrix or graph by saying that it should not contain another minimally nonlinear matrix or graph $G$, we should also check if the statement to be proved still holds for $G$. The exception of $R$ above is a good example.

[quote=]

Here are a few more questions related to these results:

What is an upper bound on the number of edges in any separated minimally non-linear bipartite ordered graph that has $k$ total vertices (including the vertices in both parts)?

Let the first and second part has $w$ and $h$ vertices, i.e. $w+h=k$. $|E(G)|$ is bounded by $2h+w$ and $2w+h$. So $|E(G)| \leq k+\min(w,h)\leq 3k/2$.

[quote=]
What is a lower bound on the number of edges in any separated minimally non-linear bipartite ordered graph that has $k$ total vertices (including the vertices in both parts)?

$|E(G)|\geq\max(w,h)\geq k/2$.

What is a lower bound on the number of ones in any minimally non-linear $0-1$ matrix with $k$ rows?
[/quote]
A naive bound is $k$.

[/quote]
Yes, but could be naively improved to $2\sum_{i=\lceil (k+2)/4 \rceil}^{4k-2}(2^{k}-1)^{i}$

problem_text: What is $f_k(n)$, the minimum number of edges in a $k$-uniform hypergraph with $n$ vertices such that every $k$-uniform hypergraph with $n$ vertices and at least $f_k(n)$ edges is cop-win?

posts.title: Cop-win graphs based on number of edges
posts.text:
[quote=][quote=]
Now that we���ve settled this, does anyone have other ideas we can characterize cop-robber graphs based on number of edges? Or should we look somewhere else?[/quote]

Here is one extension of the edge idea. Consider the cop-robber game on a $k$-uniform hypergraph, so that both players can move from vertex $u$ to vertex $v$ if some edge contains both $u$ and $v$. Define $f_{k}(n)$ to be minimal so that every $k$-uniform hypergraph with $n$ vertices and at least $f_{k}(n)$ edges is cop-win, so $f(n) = f_{2}(n)$. 

What is $f_{k}(n)$ for all $k$ and $n$?[/quote]

Let the edges of the hypergraph be denoted $E_1 \ldots E_n.$   If $E_i, E_j$ have a non-empty intersection, it makes no sense for the cop or the robber to be in $E_i$ and none of the other edges, because it limits their access.  Therefore we can ignore all nodes which are in only one edge.  Likewise, it makes no sense for the cop or robber to be in $E_i \cap E_j$ and no other edges, if there is a $k$ such that $E_i \cap E_j \cap E_k$ is non-empty. 

If we delete all nodes that are only in a group of edges that has a non-empty intersection with another edge, we get only various "clusters" of nodes left over.  If we then make a new graph with vertices representing these clusters and edges connecting clusters between which the cop and robber can transfer in one move, we have a new game of cops and robbers that equivalent to the old game if the players play optimally, but is not on a hypergraph.

problem_text: What is $f(n)$, the minimum number of edges such that every $n$-vertex graph with at least $f(n)$ edges is cop-win?

posts.title: Cop-win graphs based on number of edges
posts.text:
Idea: intuitively, the more edges a graph has, the easier it is for the cop to win. 

Let $f(n)$ be the largest number such that there is all graphs with $n$ vertices and at least $f(n)$ edges are cop-win.

On the upper bound, for example, $K_n$ is easily a cop-win graph. We can go further: a graph with $n$ vertices that has a vertex of degree $n-1$ is also a cop-win graph. (Here and for the rest of this post I will not count loops.) Thus, any graph which has at least $\frac{n(n-2)}{2} + 1$ edges is cop-win, so we get the straightforward bound $$f(n) \leq \frac{n(n-2)}{2} + 1.$$

For the lower bound, here is a construction of a robber-win graph with lots of edges. The idea is to use Nowakowski���s Corollary from Theorem 1: use the direct product of $C_4$ and $P_k$, giving a graph with $4k$ vertices and $8k^2 - 8k + 4$ edges. Thus $$f(n) \geq \frac{n^2 - 4n + 8}{2} + 1.$$

These aren���t very good bounds, but they kinda sorta work. Does this look like a good way to characterize cop-robber graphs, or should we try something else?

posts.title: Cop-win graphs based on number of edges
posts.text:
In fact $f(n)$ is exactly $\left \lfloor \frac{n(n-2)}{2} +1 \right \rfloor$, as any graph with $n$ vertices and $\left \lfloor \frac{n(n-2)}{2} +1 \right \rfloor$ contain a vertex with degree $n-1$, and it is possible to construct a graph with $\left \lfloor \frac{n(n-2)}{2} \right \rfloor$ edges that is robber-win.

[hide=n even]
For $n$ even, let $n=2k$. Consider the graph $G$ that is the complete graph $K_n$ minus a perfect matching. This graph contain $\frac{2k(2k-1)}{2}-k=\frac{n(n-2)}{2}$ edges. We call two vertices opposite to each other if they are not adjacent in $G$. Each vertex will be opposite to exactly one other vertex. For each vertex $v$, denote the vertex opposite $v$ by $v'$.
The robber's strategy is to always move to (or choose in the first turn) a vertex opposite to the cop's vertex.
This is always possible as at before each turn of the cop, the cop and robber are on opposite vertices (from the previous turn) - say the cop is on $v_m$ and the robber is on $v_m'$, and that the cop moves to $v_{m+1}$. Clearly $v_{m+1}\neq v_m'$ as $v_m'$ and $v_m$ are opposite. Therefore $v_{m+1}'\neq v_m$, thus the robber can move to $v_{m+1}'$.
[/hide]

[hide=n odd]
For $n$ odd, let $n=2k+1$. Consider the same graph $G$ as when $n=2k$, and add a vertex with degree $2k-1$ - this vertex is adjacent to all other vertices except one which we will call $a$. This graph has $\frac{2k(2k-2)}{2}+(2k-1)=\frac{n(n-2)-1}{2}$ edges.
We use the same opposite definition as when $n$ is even; notice that all vertices except $a$ is opposite to exactly one other vertex, and $a$ is opposite to two other vertices, which we will call $a_1$ and $a_2$.
Let the symbol $x\leftrightarrow y$ means that $x$ is opposite $y$.
The robber's strategy here is as follows:
> In the first turn, choose a vertex opposite to the cop's vertex.
> In subsequent turns, assume that the robber starts the turn at $w_m$ opposite to the cop at $v_m$. Let the cop moves from $v_m$ to $v_{m+1}$. As $v_m\leftrightarrow w_m$, $v_{m+1}\neq w_m$. We claim that the robber can move from $w_m$ to a point $w_{m+1}$ opposite $v_{m+1}$.
1. If $w_m\neq a$ and $w_m\not\leftrightarrow a$, the robber can move to all points except $v_m$. Since $v_{m+1}\neq w_m$, $v_{m+1} \not\leftrightarrow v_m$, thus the robber can move to the point opposite $v_{m+1}$.
2. If $w_m = a$, WLOG $v_m=a_1$. The robber can move to all vertices except $a_1$ and $a_2$. Since $v_{m+1} \neq a$, the point opposite $v_{m+1}$ is neither $a_1$ nor $a_2$, thus the robber can move to that point.
3. If $w_m = a_1$ or $a_2$ then $v_m=a$. The robber can move to all vertices except $a$. Since $v_{m+1}$ is neither $a_1$ nor $a_2$, the point opposite $v_{m+1}$ is not $a$, thus the robber can move to that point.

In all cases, the robber can move to the point opposite to $v_{m+1}$, thus by induction, the robber can always escape from the cop.
[/hide]

EDIT: see generalization at [url=http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/polymath/mitprimes2017a/f/c382892h1365138_specific_coprobber_graph_families]post #3 here.[/url]

problem_text: Given fixed starting positions for $k$ cops on a connected graph, what is an optimal pursuit algorithm for $k$ cops versus the known gambler that minimizes expected capture time?

posts.title: Computing optimal strategy w/ multiple cops and known gamble
posts.text:
So far we've been assuming gambler employs optimal distribution, i.e. optimal gamble. However, what if the gamble is not optimal? What is then the optimal strategy for cop?

In the paper below, the author proposed two algorithms to compute optimal cop strategy given any gamble. Interestingly, I think it could extend to the case with multiple cops. Does anyone see how to do it?

http://arxiv.org/abs/1701.00187

posts.title: Computing optimal strategy w/ multiple cops and known gamble
posts.text:
With multiple cops, one issue is choosing the initial positions. If they all start from the same position, the worst-case expected capture time is still $n$ for some connected $n$-vertex graphs, e.g. $P_{n}$ when they start at one end and the gambler sits at the other.

Lemma 1 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1610.02724v1.pdf can be used to choose the initial positions for the cops, but in general it will not be optimal. If anyone sees a way to improve Lemma $1$, I think this will help to find an improved strategy for $k$ cops.

posts.title: Computing optimal strategy w/ multiple cops and known gamble
posts.text:
[quote=]So far we've been assuming gambler employs optimal distribution, i.e. optimal gamble. However, what if the gamble is not optimal? What is then the optimal strategy for cop?

In the paper below, the author proposed two algorithms to compute optimal cop strategy given any gamble. Interestingly, I think it could extend to the case with multiple cops. Does anyone see how to do it?

http://arxiv.org/abs/1701.00187[/quote]
I assume that for each turn, only one cop can move.  However, it is not too difficult to write a variant where all cops can choose to move in the same turn.

Let there be $k$ cops, and let $T\left(t_1, \ldots, t_k \right)$ be the optimal expected chase time when the cops enter vertices $t_1, \ldots, t_k.$ Note that these vertices do not have to be distinct.   Also let ${v_i}(S)=1$ if and only if $v_i \in S,$ else ${v_i}(S)=0.$  Finally, let $E_k(G)$ be the set of tuples of tuples $\left((t_{11}, t_{12}, \ldots, t_{1k}), (t_{21}, t_{22}, \ldots, t_{2k}), \right)$ such that there exists exactly one $i$ such that $t_{1i} \ne t_{2i}$ and for this unique $i,$ $(t_{1i}, t_{2i}) \in E(G).$

Then, the following algorithm evaluates $T\left(t_1, \ldots, t_k \right).$

[indent]
[b]for all $t_1 , \ldots , t_k \in \left(V(G)\right)^k$ do[/b]
[indent]
$T\left(t_1 , \ldots , t_k\right) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} {v_i \left(\left\{t_1, \ldots , t_k \right \} \right) \cdot p_i},~ \pi(t_1 , \ldots , t_k)=\left(t_1 , \ldots , t_k \right).$
[/indent]
[b]end for[/b]
$S = \left(V(G)\right)^k$
[b]while $\left|S\right| > 0$ do[/b]
[indent]
$u = \arg \min_{t \in S} T(t)$
$S = S - u$
[b]for all $w \in S$ such that $\left(w, u\right) \in E_k(G)$ do[/b]
[indent]
[b]if $T(w) > 1 + \left(1-\sum_{i=1}^{n} {v_i \left(\left\{u_1, \ldots , u_k \right \} \right) \cdot p_i}\right) T(u)$ then[/b]
[indent]
$T(w) = 1 + \left(1-\sum_{i=1}^{n} {v_i \left(\left\{u_1, \ldots , u_k \right \} \right) \cdot p_i}\right) T(u)$
$\pi(w) = u$
[/indent]
[b]end if[/b]
[/indent]
[b]end for[/b]
[/indent]
[b]end while[/b]
[/indent]

posts.text:
[quote=]With multiple cops, one issue is choosing the initial positions. If they all start from the same position, the worst-case expected capture time is still $n$ for some connected $n$-vertex graphs, e.g. $P_{n}$ when they start at one end and the gambler sits at the other.

Lemma 1 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1610.02724v1.pdf can be used to choose the initial positions for the cops, but in general it will not be optimal. If anyone sees a way to improve Lemma $1$, I think this will help to find an improved strategy for $k$ cops.[/quote]

Yes, Lemma 1 provides a good way to find good initial position for cop. The algorithms I mentioned (and the one for multiple cops that I have in mind) take any initial position, including multiple cops on the same vertex. So these algorithms and Lemma 1 shall be complimentary to each other.

However, is taking the $k$ most likely vertices in the beginning and then stay there forever optimal for $k$ cops? Assume the gamble is static.

On the other hand, if the gamble is unknown, it'll be interesting to ask what is the optimal initial position over all possible gambles, which is purely based on graph structure. I wonder what optimality or good property about Lemma 1 could we prove.

We use a Fibonacci heap to store $S.$ Because we're using a Fibonacci heap to store $S,$ removing and storing $u=\arg \min_{t \in S} T(t)$ takes $O(|S|)=O(\log(|V(G)|^k))$ time. Therefore, the algorithm has complexity $O(k\log(|V(G)|)|V(G)|^k+\left(|E(G)|+|V(G)|\right)^k).$

Does the probability of ending up in vertex $k$ follow from the equality case of Cauchy-Schwartz?

Also, could you provide a similar explanation for the hypnotist?[/quote]

No, it follows from [url=https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c382892h1468127]definition[/url]:

[quote=]In that case, the relative probaility $P_v$ of ending up on a given adjacent or the original vertex $v$ is proportional to the illusionist's probability of not appearing at that vertex; specifically, given $V$ the set of adjacent vertices and the original vertex, we have
$$P_v = \frac{1-p_v}{\sum\limits_{k \in V}{1-p_k}}$$[/quote]

For the hypnotist:

[quote=]$$T(v) =
\begin{cases}
1 + (1-p)(1 - p_v)\min_{u \in N(v)}T(u) + \frac{p\sum_{k \in V} p_kT(k)}{\sum_{k \in V} p_k} & \text{if } \sum_{k \in V} p_k \neq 0,\\
1 + (1 - p_v)\min_{u \in N(v)}T(u) & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}$$[/quote]

By definition, if the sum of the probabilities of the hypnotist appearing in $V$ is zero, then the cop goes to whichever vertex she wants. This gives the second part, which is essentially the same with the gambler. Otherwise, the cop gets confused with probability $p$; the expected number of moves in whatever new vertex $k$ she ends up in is $T(k)$; she ends up in that vertex with probability $\frac{p_k}{\sum p_k}$. If she doesn���t get confused, with probability $1-p$, she does what she wants. Then take the expected value.

posts.text:
In parityhome���s paper https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.00187 (section 2.2), an algorithm similar to Djikstra���s algorithm is used to find the cop���s best strategy in the gambler pursuit game. [b]If the algorithm is modified as described below, does it work in general for calculating any $T(v)$ with the following form?[/b]

EDIT: replaced with parityhome's suggestion

[quote=]$T(v)=\min(J(v), \min_{u\in N(v)}H(v,u))$ where $J(v)$ serves as initilization, e.g. $1/p_v$, and $H(v,u)$ is a general function that could implicitly use $T(u)$ as well.

I think this is the requirement for generalized Dijkstra algorithm to work:

If $T(v)=H(v,u)$ where $u\in N(v)$, then $T(v)\geq T(u)$. I.e. when we update $t(v)$ based on $u$, $t(v)\geq t(u)$. Put it in another way, as we go along a chase path $T(v)$ never increases.

For the minimal expected capture time $T(v)$ of the regular gambler when the cop starts from vertex $v$, it looks like $H(v,u) = 1+(1-p_v)T(u)$ and $J(v) = 1/p_v$.
For $T(v)$ when there is wait time $n(v,u)$ on each edge for the cop, it looks like $H(v,u) = 1+(1-p_v)(n(v, u)+T(u))$ and $J(v) = 1/p_v$.
For the minimal probability of evasion in $m$ turns $e(m, v)$ when the cop starts from vertex $v$ and edges have no wait time, I think $H(v,u) = (1-p_v)e(m-1,u)$ and $J(v) = (1-p_v)^{m}$.
Anyone see issues with the functions above?
Also does anyone see how to get $e(m, v)$ when there is wait time $n(v,u)$ on each edge for the cop?

[quote=][quote=][quote=]$T(v) = min(F(v, G(u)),T(v))$ with $u = argmin_{v \in S} G(v)$, such that $F(x,y)$ is any real-valued function with first input a vertex and second input a real number, and $G$ is a real-valued function with one vertex input.[/quote]
The sentence above is replaced with this sentence:

$T(v) = min(F(v, G(u)),T(v))$ over all $u$ with $(v, u) \in E$, such that $F(x,y)$ is any real-valued function with first input a vertex and second input a real number, $G$ is a real-valued function with one vertex input, and $argmin_{v \in S_{i}} G(v) = argmin_{v \in S_{i}} T(v)$ for all $i \geq 0$.

In the generalized Djikstra algorithm, the line $u = argmin_{v \in S} T(v)$ in parityhome���s paper would be replaced with $u = argmin_{v \in S} G(v)$.[/quote]

I would formulate as this:

$T(v)=\min(J(v), \min_{u\in N(v)}H(v,u))$ where $J(v)$ serves as initilization, e.g. $1/p_v$, and $H(v,u)$ is a general function that could implicitly use $T(u)$ as well. (Having $T(v)=\min(T(v),\ldots)$ may be more suitable for algorithmic description.)

I think this is the requirement for generalized Dijkstra algorithm to work:

If $T(v)=H(v,u)$ where $u\in N(v)$, then $T(v)\geq T(u)$. I.e. when we update $t(v)$ based on $u$, $t(v)\geq t(u)$. Put it in another way, as we go along a chase path $T(v)$ never increases.[/quote]

posts.text:
[quote=]Is it true that all graphs representable as compact visibility graphs in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ are also representable as compact visibility graphs in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$?[/quote]

Let $B(x_1,x_2,y_1,y_2,z_1,z_2)$ be the 3-dimentional rectangular prism bounded between [center]$x=x_1, x=x_2, y=y_1, y=y_2, z=z_1,$ and $z=z_2.$[/center]
Consider the compact visibility graph formed by the following eight rectangular prisms: $$\begin{array}{rrrrrrr} 
B(&\!0.0,&\!1.0,&\!0.0,&\!1.0,&\!0.0,&\!1.0)\\\\
B(&\!\!\!\!\!\!-0.4,&\!\!\!\!\!\!-0.2,&\!\!\!\!\!\!-0.4,&\!\!\!\!\!\!-0.2,&\!\!\!\!\!\!-0.4,&\!\!\!\!\!\!-0.2)\\\\
B(&\!\!\!\!\!\!-0.4,&\!\!\!\!\!\!-0.2,&\!0.4,&\!0.8,&\!0.4,&\!0.8)\\\\
B(&\!0.4,&\!0.8,&\!\!\!\!\!\!-0.4,&\!\!\!\!\!\!-0.2,&\!0.4,&\!0.8)\\\\
B(&\!0.4,&\!0.8,&\!0.4,&\!0.8,&\!\!\!\!\!\!-0.4,&\!\!\!\!\!\!-0.2)\\\\
B(&\!1.4,&\!1.6,&\!0.4,&\!0.6,&\!0.4,&\!0.6)\\\\
B(&\!0.4,&\!0.6,&\!1.4,&\!1.6,&\!0.4,&\!0.6)\\\\
B(&\!0.4,&\!0.6,&\!0.4,&\!0.6,&\!1.4,&\!1.6)
\end{array}$$

According to [url=https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/bbb8/6f4c0a26c38ec27e91ca9398e5482e2bad5a.pdf]A General Notion of Vibibility Graphs[/url], Figure 7 is not a 2-dimentional convex compact visibility graph. However, this is a 3-dimentional convex compact visibility graph.

Therefore, [b]not[/b] all graphs representable as [b][u]convex[/u][/b] compact visibility graphs in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ are representable as [b][u]convex[/u][/b] compact visibility graphs in $\mathbb{R}^{2}.$

Excellent construction user! In fact, using Corollary 1 of the paper, we can find a smaller example with six regions: consider three spheres of radius slightly less than one centered at $(0, 0, 0)$, $(0, 0, -2)$, $(0, 0, 2)$, and three spheres of radius slightly more than zero at $(1, 1, 0)$, $(0, -1, 0)$, $(-1, 0, 0)$. (This is minimal; any graph with five vertices is either planar or is $K_5$, which in turn contains $K_4$.)

Each of the small spheres are visible to each large sphere, so $K_{3, 3}$ is a subgraph, so it is not planar. Consider any set of four vertices, if at least two of the small spheres were in it they can���t be a $K_4$ because no two small spheres are visible to each other. The only choice for a $K_4$ would be one small sphere and three large spheres, but the top and bottom large spheres are not visible to each other. 

I���m wondering if we can extend Corollary 1 to compact $k$-visibility graphs, but I don���t know what its analogue would be. If we can find such a forbidden characterization, then perhaps it is possible to construct convex compact $k$-visibility graphs in $\mathbb{R}^3$ not representable as convex compact $k$-visibility graphs in $\mathbb{R}^2$ as user did.

[rule]
Let's fix post #10. The corollary does not follow from edge-connectedness, rather the other way around:

Every edge in a compact $k$-visibility graph with at least $k+2$ vertices is part of some $K_{k+2}$. [hide=Sketch]
Consider two mutually $\ell$-visible regions $A, B$. Consider the $k-\ell$ nearest regions to $A \cup B$, label them $C_1, \ldots, C_{k-\ell}$ from nearest to farthest. We claim region $C_i$ is at most $\ell+i-1$-visible to one and at most $\ell+i$-visible to the other. Suppose it were not $\ell+i-1$ visible to either, then it can't be the $\ell+i$th nearest. Then it's $\ell+i-1$ visible to WLOG $A$, and since $A$ is $\ell$-visible to $B$, the sightline connecting $B$ to $C_i$ can���t intersect any other region except $A$, the at most $\ell$ regions blocked by a sightline from $B$ to $A$, or the $C_j$ with $j < i$, otherwise it���s not the $i$th nearest. Thus it���s at most $\ell+i$-visible to $B$.

To complete, consider two mutually zero-visible regions, consider the $k$ nearest regions to their union, and apply the above claim to each pair of them. This shows these are all connected to each other. Thus all edges are part of a $K_{k+2}$.
[/hide]

Corollary: A compact $k$-visibility graph with at least $k+2$ vertices is $k+1$-edge-connected. [hide=Sketch]Apply above result. Alternatively use proof from post #10.[/hide]

Wait, from Corollary 2 in the paper we know all trees are representable as compact zero-visibility graphs. Whoops.

We can also get a stupid bound for four-partite graphs: consider the bipyramid, it has $3n-6$ edges, and is representable by Theorem 4. I don���t think we can get a bound of $O(n^2)$, but that���s just what I feel.

problem_text: Is a compact $k$-visibility graph with at least $k+2$ vertices always $(k+1)$-edge-connected?

posts.title: compact visibility graphs
posts.text:
Not exactly sure: none of the edges are bridges for $k = 1$. Maybe even better: a compact $k$-visible graph is $k+1$-edge-connected.

For $k = 1$, if we have at least three regions, the graph is two-edge-connected. [hide=Sketch]
Consider any two mutually zero-visible regions $A, B$. Then any region $C$ zero-visible to one is at most one-visible to the other. Clearly $C$ must exist (this is the only hand-wavy part I think). So two distinct paths connect them: $A-B$ and $A-C-B$. So disconnecting $A-B$ won't disconnect the graph, so it's not a bridge.

Now consider two mutually one-visible regions $A, B$. Any one-sightline from $A$ to $B$ passes through a different region, call it $C$. Then $C$ is zero-visible to both. Again, two distinct paths connect them: $A-B$ and $A-C-B$, so $A-B$ isn't a bridge. But we have now considered all edges in the graph and shown that none of them are bridges, so the graph is two-edge-connected.
[/hide]

Similarly, a compact $k$-visible graph is $k+1$-edge-connected. [hide=Sketch]
Do a similar proof to the above.
[/hide]
[i]Corollary:[/i] (wait, is this the right direction?) Every edge in a compact $k$-visibility graph is a part of some $K_k$.

problem_text: In the cop-killer game, are all trees that are not stars killer-win?

posts.title: Cop-and-killer game
posts.text:
Consider the following generalization of the cop-and-robber game which is more symmetric. Our two players are now a [i]cop[/i] and a [i]killer[/i], also a perfect information game. The cop picks a vertex and the killer also picks a vertex. Then the game begins, with the cop going first. He moves to an adjacent vertex, followed by the killer moving to an adjacent vertex. If after the cop moves he occupies the vertex the killer is located, he wins. Similarly, if after the killer moves, she occupies the vertex the cop is located, she wins. If neither happens after a finite amount of turns, it is a stalemate. 

Some initial results.

Clearly all graphs with a universal vertex are cop-win.

All trees which are not stars are killer-win.
[hide=Sketch]
Suppose the cop has picked a vertex, which we will root the tree at. The killer picks a vertex with distance two to the vertex the cop picked, which is possible as the tree is not a star. When the game begins, after each cop move, the killer moves toward the cop (there is only one possible move); thus the distance between them after this is still two, assuming the cop does not move backwards. The cop can only move forward for a finite number of moves as the graph does not contain a cycle, so eventually he will reach a leaf node. The cop then moves away from the leaf node, and is adjacent to the killer, after which the killer moves to the cop���s vertex and wins.
[/hide]
(A cop-win graph in the dismantlable sense is not always a cop-win graph in the cop-killer sense.)

Clearly the triangle is cop-win. Also, the four-cycle is killer-win. Cycles with more than five vertices are stalemate graphs.
[hide=Sketch]For the former, the killer picks the opposite corner of the four-cycle and wins next turn. For the latter, killer picks vertex of distance two from cop, and moves so that they are never adjacent, neither player can win.[/hide]
(This is clearly different from the cop-robber game, in that the killer wins in the four-cycle.)

Grid graphs are killer-win, but king's graphs (with dimension at least two) are stalemate graphs.
[hide=Sketch]For the former, killer chooses opposite corner of a four-cycle the cop is currently in. Killer mirrors cop's moves, maintaining distance two until cop is forced into corner, in which case killer wins next turn. For the latter, each player just maintains distance two from the other.[/hide]
(Direct products don���t seem to have any connection, unlike cop-robber graphs.)

Well, a bipartite graph is cop-win iff it is the claw. Sufficiency is vacuous, for necessity suppose it were not the claw, the killer merely picks any vertex in the same set the cop picks. At the start of each of the cop���s turns the killer is in the same set he is, so he can never catch her.

problem_text: For each $m \geq 1$, do there exist non-bipartite killer-win graphs in the cop-killer game that are $C_{2k+1}$-free for each $1 \leq k \leq m$?

posts.title: Cop-and-killer game
posts.text:
[quote=]
These constructions are awesome, user. Are there both cop-win and killer-win graphs with exactly one triangle? What about $k$ triangles?
[/quote]
Consider the wheel, which is cop-win and can have arbitrarily many triangles. Not sure about killer-win.

[quote=]
Also, are there any killer-win triangle-free graphs that are non-bipartite?[/quote]
[img]http://i.imgur.com/SSWU8dr.png[/img]

Some progress on the second question lead me to this. We use the notation from here:
[quote=]
Also inspired by Nowakowski, we can do something like dismantling. Say vertex $u$ [i]covers[/i] a vertex $v$ if $N(v) \subseteq N(u)$. We have the following result. (Note that this condition is not sufficient: join a $C_5$ and a $C_4$ with a bridge.)

A graph is a non-stalemate graph only if it has a universal vertex or one vertex covers another. [hide=Sketch]
Consider the ultimate move, whence the winning player moves to the vertex of the losing player. Then the penultimate move would be the losing player being forced to move to a vertex adjacent to the winning player; otherwise the losing player would move to a non-adjacent vertex and prolong the game. Thus the existence of a vertex covering another (or a universal vertex, have to rule out this case) is necessary.
[/hide][/quote]

I think it's important to make clear that $N(v)$ here is the [i]open[/i] neighbor set, it does not include the vertex itself. The following is quite unsure:

A graph with girth at least $5$ is stalemate. [hide=Sketch]
Suppose it were not stalemate, therefore one vertex covers another. If vertex $u$ covers vertex $v$, that means that that there exists two distinct common neighbors $v', v''$, and then $u-v'-v-v''-u$ is a four-cycle. Only need to rule out the case when all pairs of covering vertices have only one path between them, not exactly sure how to do this.
[/hide]

Woops, I found an error in my proof in post #59.  Here is a corrected statement:

[indent]
Let $G$ and $H$ be connected graphs such that $|H|>1$ and $G$ is not a tree; then I claim $G \square H$ is a stalemate.
[/indent]

[b]Proof.[/b]
[indent]
Let $u, w$ be connected vertices in $H,$ and let $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n$ be a cycle in $G.$ Then, either player can remain among vertices of the form $(v_i, u)$ and $(v_i, w)$ forever.  This is because $(v_i, u)$ is the only vertex adjacent to all of $(v_{i-1},u),$ $(v_{i+1},u),$ and $(v_i, w),$ and likewise, $(v_i, w)$ is the only vertex adjacent all of $(v_{i-1}, w),$ $(v_{i+1}, w)$ and $(v_i, u).$  Therefore, neither player can be cornered out of their "safe zone", and so can forever avoid losing.
[/indent]

I was waiting for you to reply :) This is a great result. Perhaps it can be applied to the original cop-robber problem to get a new characterization?

Here are some observations I made today, both inspired by Nowakowski���s results:

Cop-win, killer-win and stalemate graphs are all non-retract-closed. $C_4$ retracts to $P_3$, the former is killer-win and the latter is cop-win. Also $C_6$, stalemate, retracts to $P_4$. Products also don���t seem to help much as our graphs are non-reflexive unlike Nowakowski ��� if not moving on a turn was allowed, then all games would end with a stalemate. However, we can still get a homomorphism-related result:

A graph homomorphic to a graph such that each image has at least two distinct vertices in its pre-image is non-cop-win. [hide=Sketch]
Killer picks vertex in pre-image of cop's vertex. In her turn, she moves to an adjacent vertex with the same image as the cop���s. The cop never ends his turn at the killer���s vertex so he never wins.
[/hide]
(are there other results based on homomorphisms? perhaps we can get a result based on graph products, but probably not as strong as nowakowski���s result on cop-robber graphs)

Also inspired by Nowakowski, we can do something like dismantling. Say vertex $u$ [i]covers[/i] a vertex $v$ if $N(v) \subseteq N(u)$. We have the following result. (Note that this condition is not sufficient: join a $C_5$ and a $C_4$ with a bridge.)

A graph is a non-stalemate graph only if it has a universal vertex or one vertex covers another. [hide=Sketch]
Consider the ultimate move, whence the winning player moves to the vertex of the losing player. Then the penultimate move would be the losing player being forced to move to a vertex adjacent to the winning player; otherwise the losing player would move to a non-adjacent vertex and prolong the game. Thus the existence of a vertex covering another (or a universal vertex, have to rule out this case) is necessary.
[/hide]
(perhaps we can extend this idea to get a dismantling order? i can���t figure this out ��� one idea is to consider the graph with the same vertices, except replace the edges with directed edges representing covering. then trace a path or something, i couldn���t get this to work.)

[quote=][quote=]Consider the following generalization of the cop-and-robber game which is more symmetric.  Our two players are now a cop and a killer, also a perfect information game. The cop picks a vertex and the killer also picks a vertex. Then the game begins, with the cop going first. He moves to an adjacent vertex, followed by the killer moving to an adjacent vertex. If after the cop moves he occupies the vertex the killer is located, he wins. Similarly, if after the killer moves, she occupies the vertex the cop is located, she wins. If neither happens after a finite amount of turns, it is a stalemate.[/quote]

I ran a simulation in Python, with total sample size of $2^{20}=1,048,576$ plays and printing intermediate results every $1024$ plays.   In each play, there were $20$ vertices and a $50\%$ chance than a given pair of vertices were connected${}^{*}.$  Each player started in optimal position and played optimally. posts.text:
[quote=]
The probability that $G_{n}$ has a universal vertex goes to $0$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. Is it possible to show the probability that there exist $u$ and $v \in V(G_{n})$ such that $N(u) \subset N(v)$ also goes to $0$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$?[/quote]

Consider a random graph $G$ with $n+1$ vertices. Suppose the probability two given vertices are connected is $p$, independently.

We compute the expected number of ordered pairs $(u, v) \in V(G_n)$ such that $N(u) \subseteq N(v)$. This is easier to compute because of linearity of expectation: this is $(n+1)n$ times the probability that a given vertex $v$ covers another vertex $u$.

But this is the probability each neighbor of $u$ is also a neighbor of $v$, which is $p^{|N(u)|}$. Now we need $E[p^{|N(u)|}]$. Let $X = |N(u)|$. The number of $u$'s neighbors is a binomial random variable, so $X \sim B(n,p)$. 

Then $E[p^X] = E[e^{X\ln p}]$. But this is the moment generating function $M_X(\ln p)$ which is $\left(pe^{\ln p} + 1 - p\right)^n$ or $\left(p^2 - p + 1\right)^n$. 

The final expectation is $(n+1)n\left(p^2 - p + 1\right)^n$. If $p \in (0, 1)$ then $0 < p^2 - p + 1 < 1$. Taking the limit as $n \to \infty$ makes it zero.

I���m not so sure of the above logic: the sketchy part is $E[p^X]$ being the expectation of the indicator. Some slack can be afforded if it should be $\binom{n}{2}$ instead of $(n+1)n$, and if the MGF doesn���t hold for integral values; a similar derivation should work.

problem_text: In the cop-killer game, for graphs $G$ and $H$ with $|G|, |H| > 1$, is $G \times H$ killer-win if and only if at least one of $G$ or $H$ is killer-win?

posts.title: Cop-and-killer game
posts.text:
[quote=]
Let $G$ and $H$ be connected graphs such that $|H|>1$ and $G$ is not a tree; then I claim $G \square H$ is a stalemate.
[/quote]

It is helpful to think of the tensor product of two graphs as two separate games being played simultaneously. Then we have:

For any two graphs $|G|>1$ and $|H|>1,$ $G\times H$
[list]
[*]is a stalemate iff both are not killer-win,
[*]is killer-win iff at least one is killer-win.
[/list]
For my first claim, let the cop choose $(g,h)\in G\times H$ to start. The killer cannot lose by choosing $(g,h')\in G\times H$ and matching the cop's first coordinate every move thereafter. The cop cannot lose by playing optimally on both coordinates, as the killer cannot match both coordinates.

For my second claim, WLOG $H$ is killer-win. Let the cop choose $(g,h)\in G\times H$ to start. The killer wins by choosing $(g,h')\in G\times H$ where $h'$ is the optimal response to $h$ in $H,$ and matching the cop's first coordinate every move thereafter while playing optimally on the second coordinate.

Let $G$ and $H$ be connected graphs such that $G$ and $H$ each have an edge, and $G$ has no universal vertices. Then $G\boxtimes H$ is a stalemate, as there are no universal vertices, nor are there corners (i.e. non-adjacent vertices, one of which covers the other) in this graph.
-----
Let $G$ and $H$ be connected graphs with $|G|>1$ and $|H|>1.$ Now we have:
[list]
[*]$G~\square~ H$ is a stalemate if at least one of $G$ and $H$ is not a tree.
[*]$G\times H$ is a stalemate iff both $G$ and $H$ are not killer-win, and killer-win otherwise.
[*]$G\boxtimes H$ is cop-win iff both $G$ and $H$ have a universal vertex, and is stalemate otherwise. 
[/list]

problem_text: In the cop-killer game, which outcome classes (cop-win, killer-win, stalemate) are closed under the Cartesian product, tensor product, and strong product?

[list]

problem_text: In the $k$ cop and pilferer game, is every graph $G$ that is robber-win in the infinite cop-robber game also pilferer-win for any number of turns $k$?

posts.title: Cop and Pilferer
posts.text:
Consider a perfect information game that I've named "[i]$k$ cop and pilferer,[/i]" defined as follows.


[indent]
A pilferer has nabbed \$100 out of someone's purse, and is being chased by a cop.  On the graph $G,$ the cop picks a vertex from which to start, and the pilferer chooses another.  They take alternate turns, cop goes first.  The game has a total of $k$ turns, so the cop takes $\left\lceil \frac k 2\right\rceil$ turns and the pilferer takes $\left\lfloor \frac k 2 \right\rfloor.$ 

The pilferer knows that he will spend 3 months in jail if he gets caught, i.e. if the cop moves to his vertex.  However, he can reduce his sentence to 2 months by confessing to the cop; he does this by moving to the cop's vertex.  Of course he would like to remain free until the end of the $k$ turns, in which case he avoids jail and keeps his \$100 loot. 

To avoid having to spend time proving her case in court, the cop would prefer that the pilferer came to confess.  However she certainly does not want to fail her job by letting the pilferer go free, so if the pilferer does not come to confess, she will try to catch him herself.
[/indent]

Here are some initial results. 
[list=1]
[*]If in the [i]cop and robber[/i] game the cop cannot catch the robber within $k$ turns, she also cannot catch the pilferer in $k$ turns. The pilferer will simply follow the same strategy in both games.
[*]If $G$ is robber win in the (infinite) [i]cop and robber[/i] game, then it is also a pilferer win in the [i]$k$ cop and pilferer[/i] game for any $k$ up to infinity.
[*]If $G$ is a complete graph with at least 3 vertices, the cop's best strategy is to avoid the pilferer until her last turn, and if by then the pilferer has not confessed, to catch him at her last turn. In this case, the pilferer's best strategy is to confess as soon as possible. (If the cop were playing optimally, the pilferer could wait to confess until just before the cop's last turn, however the pilferer cannot know for sure that this is the case).
[*]If $G$ is bipartite, the pilferer should choose a vertex that is an even distance away from the cop. Unless it is a tree, he should pick a vertex of any available cycle, in which case he will avoid capture forever, and win.
[/list]

I think this game might be even more interesting on a directed graph.

posts.title: Cop and Pilferer
posts.text:
[i]I���m assuming we are allowing reflexive moves[/i]. It seems quite similar to the cop-and-robber game. Both players prefer the pilferer confessing over the cop catching the pilferer, so if we consider both end states equivalent we are reduced to the cop-robber game:

A graph is $k$-pilferer-win iff it is $k$-robber-win. [hide=Sketch]Sufficiency shown above. For necessity, suppose a graph is $k$-pilferer win, the robber follows the same strategy and does not get caught.[/hide]

(less sure about this) The $k$-pilferer cannot avoid capture iff the graph is $k$-cop-win. [hide=Sketch]By Nowakowski, the penultimate turn of a $k$-capture is the cop on a vertex that dominates the robber���s vertex. Thus in this case, the pilferer will simply confess-end. Suppose a $k$-pilferer is caught or confesses by the end of several moves. The pilferer would confess/get caught only if she has no adjacent vertex also not adjacent to the cop, thus it is necessary for the cop to be in a vertex dominating the pilferer���s.[/hide]

Thus we are left to characterizing cop-win graphs based on whether they are catch-end or confess-end. But the problem is, er, I haven't seen any catch-end graphs yet, where the pilferer does not willingly confess to the cop and gets caught instead.
