posts.title: Problem 2
posts.text:
This is my solution of Problem 2, part (a). Please let me know if there are any mistakes.

It was proven in  Theorem 3.6 of the paper "A Golbach conjecture for Laurent Series Semidomain" that if $S$ is an additively reduced and additively atomic semidomain, the following conditions are equivalent

 (1) $\mathcal{A}(S)=S^{\times}.$ 

 (2) every $f \in S[x^{\pm 1}]$ with |supp$(f)|>1$ can be expressed as the sum of at most 2 irreducibles.

Consider the additive monoid $M = \bigg\langle \bigg(\frac{3}{4}\bigg)^n \, | \, n \in \mathbb{N}_0 \bigg\rangle$. It is well know that $M$ is atomic and $\mathcal{A}(M)= \bigg\{\bigg(\frac{3}{4}\bigg)^n \, | \, n \in \mathbb{N}_0\bigg\} $. Since $M$ is also closed with respect to the usual multiplication of rational numbers, we know that $M$ is a semidomain. Now consider the multiplicative monoid $N= \bigg\langle \frac{3}{4} \bigg\rangle$. It is clear that $N$ is a multiplicative subset of $M$, and then we can consider the localization $N^{-1}M[x]$.

Claim 1: We see that $N^{-1}M= \bigg\langle \bigg(\frac{3}{4}\bigg)^n \, | \, n \in \mathbb{Z} \bigg\rangle$.

Proof: Let us consider an element $r\in N^{-1}M$. This means that there are $m \in M$ and $n \in N$ such that $r=\frac{m}{n}$. Take \[m=\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_i\bigg(\frac{3}{4}\bigg)^{c_i},\]
for some $a_1,...,a_k, c_1,..., c_k \in \mathbb{N}_0$, and we can suppose that $n = \bigg(\frac{3}{4} \bigg)^t$ for some $t \in \mathbb{N}_0$. Note that then \[r=\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_i\bigg(\frac{3}{4}\bigg)^{c_i-t}.\]

Since $c_i-t \in \mathbb{Z}$ for every $i \in [[1,k]]$, we can conclude that $r \in \bigg\langle \bigg(\frac{3}{4}\bigg)^n \, | \, n \in \mathbb{Z} \bigg\rangle$.

Suppose now that $r\in \bigg\langle \bigg(\frac{3}{4}\bigg)^n \, | \, n \in \mathbb{Z} \bigg\rangle$. We can write then $r=\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_i\bigg(\frac{3}{4}\bigg)^{z_i}$ for some $a_1,...,a_k \in \mathbb{N}_0$, and some $z_1,...,z_k \in \mathbb{Z}$. For each $z_i$ we can find some natural numbers $z'_i$ and $z''_i$ such that $z_i=z'_i-z''_i$. Then we can write \[r=\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_i \frac{\bigg(\frac{3}{4}\bigg)^{z'_i}}{\bigg(\frac{3}{4}\bigg)^{z''_i}},\]
which is clearly an element of $N^{-1}M$. 
Let us denote $S=N^{-1}M$. In the paper "Puiseux monoids and transfer isomorphism", X X proved in Proposition 3.5 that if $r\in \mathbb{Q}_{>0}$, then the additive monoid $M=\langle r^n  |  n \in \mathbb{Z} \rangle$ is atomic with $\mathcal{A}(M)=\{r^n | n \in \mathbb{Z}\} $.  Then, by the theorem mentioned above, we know that the semidomain $S[x]$ satisfies Goldbach conjecture. However $M[x]$ clearly does not satisfy it. Indeed, for every $n$ the polynomial $f=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\frac{3}{4}x^{k_i}$ cannot be expressed as the sum of $k$ or fewer irreducibles.

posts.text:
Hello @user I believe that I have taken your input into account. Here's what I've come up with. Thanks!
-----
-----
[b]Problem.[/b] Either construct or prove that it does not exist an additively reduced atomic semidomain $S$ with the following property: for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 2$, there exists $s \in S^* \setminus S^\times$ such that $2s$ cannot be written as a sum of $k$ multiplicative irreducibles for any $k \in \mathbb{N}$ with $k \le n$.
-----
-----
We construct such a semidomain. We (and as sofialetovo has previously), propose the semidomain $\boxed{S = \mathbb{N}_0[X]}$, the set of polynomials in one variable $X$ with coefficients in the non-negative integers $\mathbb{N}_0$. This is the monoid semidomain $\mathbb{N}_0[\mathbb{N}_0]$. We will prove this fact by demonstrating that $S$ possesses the required properties.
-----
[b]Lemma 1.[/b] The semidomain $S = \mathbb{N}_0[X]$ is both:
[list]
(a) additively reduced
(b) atomic
[/list]
with its multiplicative group of units being $S^\times = \{1\}$.

[i]Proof.[/i] (a) The semidomain $S$ is additively reduced. If $P(X) \in S$ satisfies $P(X) + P(X) = P(X)$, then it follows that $2P(X) = P(X)$. Writing $P(X) = \sum p_i X^i$ with $p_i \in \mathbb{N}_0$, the equality $2 \sum p_i X^i = \sum p_i X^i$ implies $2p_i = p_i$ for all coefficients $p_i$. Since $p_i$ are non-negative integers, this forces $p_i = 0$ for all $i$, and thus $P(X) = 0$.
(b) The semidomain $S$ is atomic. Its multiplicative group of units is $S^\times = \{1\}$, as $P(X)Q(X)=1$ with $P,Q \in \mathbb{N}_0[X]$ forces $P,Q$ to be the constant polynomial $1$. To show atomicity, let $P(X) \in S^* \setminus \{1\}$. If $P(X)$ is constant, $P(X)=c \in \mathbb{N}, c\ge 2$. By the FTA, $c$ is a finite product of prime numbers, which are atoms in $S$ (by Lemma 2). If $P(X)$ is non-constant, we factor it. If $P(X)$ is reducible, $P(X)=A(X)B(X)$ with $A,B \in S \setminus \{1\}$. If $A$ or $B$ is constant, factor the constant into primes. If both are non-constant, then $\deg(A) < \deg(P)$ and $\deg(B) < \deg(P)$. We continue factoring $A(X)$ and $B(X)$. Since the degree is a non-negative integer, it must strictly decrease, thus terminating in a finite number of steps.
-----
[b]Lemma 2.[/b] The set $\mathcal{A}(S)$ of multiplicative atoms in $S=\mathbb{N}_0[X]$ contains all prime numbers $p \in \mathbb{N}$ and irreducible polynomials like $X$. However, any polynomial of the form $cX^m$ where $c \in \mathbb{N}$ and $m \ge 2$ is multiplicatively reducible in $S$.

[i]Proof.[/i] We use the standard definiton of atoms: elements $a \in S^* \setminus \{1\}$ such that $a=bc$ implies $b=1$ or $c=1$. If $p$ is a prime number, and $p = P(X)Q(X)$ in $S$, then $P(X)=c$ and $Q(X)=d$ for $c, d \in \mathbb{N}_0$. Since $p=cd$, we know that $c=1$ or $d=1$; thus, primes are atoms. If $X = A(X)B(X)$ in $S$, then the degree of the product must equal $\deg(X)=1$. Since $\deg(A(X)B(X)) = \deg(A(X)) + \deg(B(X))$ and degrees are non-negative integers, we must have $\{\deg(A), \deg(B)\} = \{1, 0\}$. WLOG, assume $\deg(A)=1$ and $\deg(B)=0$. Let $A(X) = aX+b$ and $B(X)=c$, with $a,b,c \in \mathbb{N}_0$. The equation becomes $X = c(aX+b) = acX + bc$; thus trivially $ac=1$ and $bc=0$. Hence $a=1, c=1, b=0$, giving $A(X)=X$ and $B(X)=1$. Since $B(X)=1 \in S^\times$, $X$ is an atom. Now consider $cX^m$ with $c \in \mathbb{N}$ and $m \ge 2$. If $c=1$, we have $X^m = X \cdot X^{m-1}$. Since $m \ge 2$, both $X$ and $X^{m-1}$ are in $S \setminus \{1\}$ (as $m-1 \ge 1$, $X^{m-1}$ is not constant 1). Thus $X^m$ is reducible. If $c \ge 2$, we have $cX^m = c \cdot X^m$. Since $c \in S \setminus \{1\}$ (as $c\ge 2$) and $X^m \in S \setminus \{1\}$ (as $m \ge 1$), $cX^m$ is reducible. Thus, any polynomial of the form $cX^m$ with $c \in \mathbb{N}$ and $m \ge 2$ is reducible.
-----
We now establish the main property. We show that for any fixed integer $m \ge 2$, the element $s = X^m$ works for all $n$. Let $m \ge 2$ be a fixed integer. Let $s = X^m$. Since $m \ge 2$, $s = X^m \in S^* \setminus S^\times$. Consider $2s = 2X^m$. FTSOC, assume that $2X^m$ is a sum of $k$ atoms for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$:
$$ 2X^m = \sum_{j=1}^k a_j, \quad \text{where } a_j \in \mathcal{A}(S) \text{ for all } j=1, \dots, k. \quad (1) $$
-----
[b]Claim 1.[/b] None of the atoms $a_j$ in the sum (1) can be constant polynomials.

[i]Proof.[/i] Equation (1) at $X=0$ gives $0 = \sum_{j=1}^k a_j(0)$. Since each $a_j \in \mathbb{N}_0[X]$, its constant term $a_j(0) \in \mathbb{N}_0$. The sum being zero implies $a_j(0)=0$ for all $j$. If any $a_j$ were a prime number $p$, $a_j(0) := p \ge 2$, which is a contradiction. Thus, all $a_j$ must be non-constant polynomials with zero constant term.
-----
[b]Claim 2.[/b] Each atom $a_j$ in the sum (1) must be of the form $c_j X^m$ for some coefficient $c_j \in \mathbb{N}$.

[i]Proof.[/i] From Claim 1, each $a_j(X)$ must be a non-constant polynomial with $a_j(0)=0$, so we can write $a_j(X) = \sum_{i=1}^{d_j} c_{ji} X^i$ where $d_j \ge 1$. Substituting this into equation (1) gives
$$ 2X^m = \sum_{j=1}^k \left( \sum_{i=1}^{d_j} c_{ji} X^i \right) = \sum_{i \ge 1} \left( \sum_{j=1}^k c_{ji} \right) X^i. $$
Therefore, for any $i \ne m$ where $i \ge 1$, the coefficient of $X^i$ is $0$, so we have $\sum_{j=1}^k c_{ji} = 0$. Since $c_{ji} \in \mathbb{N}_0$, this implies $c_{ji}=0$ for all $j$ and all $i \ne m$. For the coefficient of $X^m$, we have $\sum_{j=1}^k c_{jm} = 2$. Therefore, each polynomial $a_j(X)$ must be of the form $a_j(X) = c_{jm} X^m$. Since $a_j$ must be non-constant (by Claim 1), $c_{jm}$ must be a positive integer, i.e., $c_{jm} \in \mathbb{N}$.

The assumption that $2X^m$ (for $m \ge 2$) is a sum of atoms $a_j$ leads to the conclusion that each $a_j$ must be of the form $c_j X^m$ for some $c_j \in \mathbb{N}$. However, Lemma 2 shows that any such polynomial $cX^m$ with $c \in \mathbb{N}$ and $m \ge 2$ is multiplicatively reducible. This contradicts the condition that each $a_j$ is an atom ($a_j \in \mathcal{A}(S)$).

The contradiction shows that $2X^m$ cannot be written as a sum of $k$ multiplicative irreducibles for any $k \ge 1$, provided $m \ge 2$.
-----

posts.title: Open Problem 2
posts.text:
I will focus on part (b) regarding the Laurent polynomial extensions of additively reduced semidomains. 

[b]Examples[/b]

One example is the semidomain $S_1$ consisting of all fractions $\frac{a}{2^b}$ with $a, b\in \mathbb{N}_0$. Due to Helfgott's proof of the ternary Goldbach conjecture ([url]https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.7748[/url]), every element of this semidomain may be expressed as the sum of $3$ irreducibles. Also, $S_1[x^{\pm 1}]$ is Goldbach since every element of $S_1$ is additively divisible by a unit. [color=#f00]Note: see posts $2$ and $3$ for discussion regarding the Goldbachness of $S_1$.[/color]

Another example is the semidomain $S_2$ of all fractions whose denominator is a positive odd integer and whose numerator is a nonnegative integer. Observe that $S_2$ does not satisfy Goldbach since $2$ and its associates are the only multiplicative irreducibles of $S_2$. However, every nonconstant polynomial in $S[x^{\pm 1}]$ can be written as the sum of two irreducibles since every element in $S_2$ is additively divisible by a unit. 

These examples show that it is possible for $S[x^{\pm 1}]$ to be Goldbach both when $S$ is Goldbach and when $S$ is not Goldbach. 

[b]Conditions on $S$[/b]

In order to better study the connection between semidomains $S$ and their Laurent polynomial extensions $S[x^{\pm 1}]$, it is useful to impose some conditions on $S$. Some common conditions to consider are additive atomicity, semisubtractivity, $(S, +)$ being antimatter/not antimatter, and being a UFS.

[b]Other Information[/b]

We require $\mathcal{A}_+(S)\subseteq S^\times$ for $S[x^{\pm 1}]$ to have a chance of being Goldbach. 

If $S$ is additively reduced, additively atomic, and $\mathcal{A}_+(S) = S^\times$, then $S$ is of the form $\mathbb{N}_0\left[x, \frac 1x, y, \frac 1y, z, \frac 1z, \ldots\right]$. Note that such $S$ are also Goldbach due to Kaplan and X ([url]https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.14888[/url]). This family of semidomains $S$ provides further examples of Goldbach semidomains whose Laurent polynomial extensions are also Goldbach semidomains.

If $S$ is semisubtractive and $(S, +)$ is not antimatter, then $S[x^{\pm 1}]$ is Goldbach since it is always possible to additively factor out a unit from any element of $S$. Also, if $S$ is additively reduced, semisubtractive, and additively Furstenberg, then $\mathcal{A}_+(S) = S^\times$ so $S[x^{\pm 1}]$ is Goldbach by Kaplan-X. 

Of note is the semidomain $S_3 = \{f(x) \in \mathbb{Z}[x^{\pm 1}]\mid (\text{trailing coefficient of }f) > 0\}\cup \{0\}$, which is additively reduced, semisubtractive, and Goldbach (but not additively Furstenberg).

We solve part (a).
--------
[b]Theorem.[/b] Let $S$ be an additively reduced Goldbach semidomain and $M$ be a nontrivial, reduced, linearly orderable monoid; if there exists an element $a \in S^* \setminus S^\times$ such that $2a$ is not a sum of two units of $S$, then the monoid semidomain $S[M]$ is not a Goldbach semidomain.

[i]Proof.[/i] An element $sx^m \in S[M]$ with $s \in S^*$ and $m \in M$ is irreducible if and only if either $s \in \mathcal{A}(S)$ and $m=0$, or $s \in S^\times$ and $m \in \mathcal{A}(M)$; we split our argument into two cases.

[u]Case 1:[/u] $M$ contains at least one atom. Let $m \in \mathcal{A}(M)$; by hypothesis, there exists $a \in S^* \setminus S^\times$ such that $2a$ is not a sum of two units of $S$. Consider the element $f:=ax^m$: because $a \notin S^\times$ and $m \in \mathcal{A}(M)$ implies $m \neq 0$, it is clear that $f$ is a nonzero nonunit of $S[M]$. Assume, towards a contradiction, that $2f$ can be written as the sum of two irreducibles in $S[M]$, say $2ax^m=g+h$ for some $g, h \in \mathcal{A}(S[M])$. Because $S$ is additively reduced, the support of a sum is the union of the supports of the summands; for the sum $g+h$ to be the monomial $2ax^m$, both $g$ and $h$ must be monomials with exponent $m$. Let $g=b_1x^m$ and $h=b_2x^m$ for some $b_1, b_2 \in S^*$: the equality becomes $(b_1+b_2)x^m=2ax^m$, which implies that $b_1+b_2=2a$. For $g=b_1x^m$ and $h=b_2x^m$ to be irreducible, their structure must match the characterization of irreducible monomials; since $m \in \mathcal{A}(M)$, we have $m \neq 0$, which implies that the coefficients $b_1$ and $b_2$ must belong to $S^\times$. The equality $b_1+b_2=2a$ then implies that $2a$ is a sum of two units of $S$: this contradicts our choice of $a$.

[u]Case 2:[/u] $M$ does not contain any atoms. Since $M$ is nontrivial, we can take an element $m \in M \setminus \{0\}$; consider again the element $f:=ax^m$, which is a nonzero nonunit. Assume, towards a contradiction, that $2f=g+h$ for some $g, h \in \mathcal{A}(S[M])$; as in the previous case, we must have $g=b_1x^m$ and $h=b_2x^m$ for some $b_1, b_2 \in S^*$. For a monomial $sx^q$ to be irreducible, either its exponent $q$ must be $0$ or an atom of $M$: in our case, the exponent is $m \neq 0$. By the hypothesis for this case, $M$ has no atoms, so $m \notin \mathcal{A}(M)$; therefore, neither of the conditions for irreducibility can be satisfied for $g=b_1x^m$ or $h=b_2x^m$. It follows that both $g$ and $h$ are reducible elements of $S[M]$: this contradicts our assumption that $g, h \in \mathcal{A}(S[M])$.

In both cases, we arrive at a contradiction; thus, $2f$ cannot be written as a sum of two irreducibles, and so $S[M]$ is not a Goldbach semidomain. $\square$

[b]Claim.[/b] Let $S$ be a nontrivial additively reduced semidomain; then the polynomial semidomain $S[x]$ is not a Goldbach semidomain.

[i]Proof.[/i] It suffices to find a nonzero nonunit element $f(x) \in S[x]$ such that $2f(x)$ is not a sum of two irreducible elements; we take any $s \in S^*$ and consider the polynomial $f(x):=sx^2$. Since $\deg(f)=2>0$ and $S[x]^\times=S^\times$, $f(x)$ is a nonzero nonunit of $S[x]$. Assume, towards a contradiction, that $2f(x)=2sx^2$ can be written as the sum of two irreducibles, say $g(x), h(x) \in \mathcal{A}(S[x])$; since $S$ is additively reduced, the supports of $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ must both be $\{x^2\}$. For the sum to be the monomial $2sx^2$, we must have $g(x)=b_1x^2$ and $h(x)=b_2x^2$ for some nonzero coefficients $b_1, b_2 \in S^*$: the equation $(b_1+b_2)x^2=2sx^2$ implies that $b_1+b_2=2s$.

However, any monomial of the form $cx^2$ with $c \in S^*$ is reducible in $S[x]$, as it admits the factorization $(cx) \cdot x$; neither $cx$ nor $x$ is a unit in $S[x]$ because their degrees are positive, so $cx^2$ is a product of two nonunits. In particular, $g(x)=b_1x^2$ and $h(x)=b_2x^2$ are reducible; this is a contradiction to our assumption that $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ are irreducible. $\square$

[b]Example.[/b] Consider the semidomain of Laurent polynomials over $\mathbb{Z}$ with a positive lowest-degree coefficient
$$S:=\{0\} \cup \left\{ \sum_{i=k}^{n} c_i y^i \in \mathbb{Z}[y^{\pm 1}] : c_k > 0 \right\};$$
this semidomain is known to be additively reduced and Goldbach. The units of the ring $\mathbb{Z}[y^{\pm 1}]$ are $\{\pm y^k : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$; the units of $S$ must be a subset of these. An element $-y^k$ is not in $S$ as its lowest-degree coefficient is negative; an element $y^k$ is in $S$, and its inverse $y^{-k}$ is also in $S$, so the units of $S$ are $S^\times=\{y^k : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$. By the preceding result, $S[x]$ is not a Goldbach semidomain; we also verify that $S$ satisfies the hypotheses of the initial theorem by taking the element $a:=2$. It is clear that $a \in S^* \setminus S^\times$; we consider the element $2a=4$. A sum of two units in $S$ has the form $y^{k_1}+y^{k_2}$ for some integers $k_1, k_2$: if $k_1=k_2$, the sum is $2y^{k_1}$, and if $k_1 \neq k_2$, the sum is a binomial, neither of which can be $4$. Thus, $4$ is not the sum of two units of $S$; the initial theorem, applied with the monoid $(\mathbb{N}_0, +)$, confirms that $S[x]$ is not a Goldbach semidomain.

Since $S$ is antimatter, there must exist an element $a_1\in S$ such that $p-a_1\in S$. Then, if $a_1-u\in S$ for $u\in S^\times$, we have that $(p-a_1)+(a_1-u)=p-u\in S$, so a unit additively divides $p$. This is a contradiction, so $a_1$ must be non-unitable. Similarly, there must exist $a_2\in S$ that additively divides $a_1$. As before, $a_2$ must be non-unitable. We can continue this process to find an infinite sequence of elements of $S$, all of which are non-unitable.

posts.title: Open Problem 2
posts.text:
A few facts about non-unitable elements: 

1. If there exist any non-unitable elements, then there exist an infinite number of non-unitable elements. 

Proof: Since $S$ is antimatter, every non-unitable element $p$ must have an additive divisor. By #2, this divisor must also be non-unitable. Continuing this process yields an infinite number of non-unitable elements. There is no "cycle" of additive divisors formed here due to the cancellativity of $(S, +)$. 

2. Every additive divisor of a non-unitable element is non-unitable. 

Proof: Since $S$ is antimatter, every non-unitable element $p$ is divisible by an element $a$ of $S$. So, $p-a\in S$. If $a$ is unitable (so there exists $u\in S^\times$ such that $a-u\in S$), we have $(p-a)+(a-u)=p-u\in S$, which contradicts the fact that $p$ is non-unitable.  

3. There exists a non-unitable element $s\in S$ such that all non-unitable elements of $S$ additively divide $s$. 

Proof: This follows from #2 and the semisubtractivity of $S$. For any $2$ non-unitable elements $p$ and $q$, either $p$ must additively divide $q$ or $q$ must additively divide $p$. This process keeps going until one final non-unitable element $s$ is reached. [color=#f00]This proof is kind of sketchy, so I'd appreciate it if someone could check this.[/color]

4. All non-unitable elements additively divide every unitable element (a unitable element is one that is additively divisible by a unit).

Proof: Let $a$ be a unitable element and $p$ be a non-unitable element. Then for some $u\in S^\times$, $a-u\in S$. If $p-a\in S$, then $p-a=p-(a-u)-u\in S$, which contradicts the fact that $p$ is non-unitable. Thus, we must have that $a-p\in S$. 

5. Let $s$ be a unitable element and $a$ be an arbitrary element of $S$. Then $s+a$ is unitable. 

Proof: Since $s$ is unitable, $s-u\in S$ for some $u\in S^\times$. Thus, $a+s-u\in S$ as well. 

I haven't been able to produce a contradiction regarding the existence of non-unitable elements in $S$, so I'm going to move forward with the assumption that they can exist. Hopefully the facts above help solve the $(p+p)x + (p+q)$ case in post $5$ or any other similar cases.

posts.text: I think part (a) of Open Problem 2 doesn't hold in general, right? If we take an additively reduced semidomain $S$ that satisfies the Goldbach property, then the polynomial extension does not satisfies the Goldbach property necessarily. Indeed, it is enough to take the element $f(x)=2ax^n$ for some $a\in S$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. It may be interesting to consider what happens in the case where $S$ is not additively reduced.

posts.text:
This paper: [url]https://www.jstor.org/stable/2160106?seq=3[/url], specifically corollary 2.8, seems quite strong. In particular, given that $S\setminus \overline{U}$ can be a $k$-ideal, it means we essentially must look for another method of solving this problem than the technique used by Kaplan and X. 

[b]Proof that $S\setminus\overline{U}$ is a $k$-ideal: [/b]

[u]$S\setminus\overline{U}$ is additively closed:[/u] For $p, q\in S\setminus\overline{U}$, assume WLOG that $p-q\in S$ due to semisubtractivity. Since $q$ must clearly be NU, we know that $u-q\in S$ for $u\in S^\times$. Now, $p-(u-q)\not\in S$ since otherwise $(p-q)+(p-(u-q))=2p-u$ would be in $S$ which is not allowed since all multiples of $p$ must be NU by definition of $S\setminus\overline{U}$. As such, $u-q-p\in S$ for all $u\in S^\times$ meaning that $p+q$ is NU. 

Since $sp, sq\in S\setminus\overline{U}$ for all $s\in S$, we can just repeat the above process with $sp$ and $sq$ to get that $sp+sq\in NU$. So, all multiples of $p+q$ are NU, which implies that $p+q\in S\setminus\overline{U}$. 

[u]$S\setminus\overline{U}$ is multiplicatively absorbing:[/u] Take $s\in \overline{U}$ and $p\in S\setminus\overline{U}$. Then $ps\in S\setminus\overline{U}$ since if $ps$ were to divide a unitable element, then $p$ would divide a unitable element -- a contradiction. 

[u]S\setminus\overline{U} is subtractive (same as a $k$-ideal since $S$ is subtractive):[/u] Say that for $q\in S$, $p, p+q\in S\setminus\overline{U}$. Then, if $q\in \overline{U}$, there must exist $s\in S$ such that $qs$ is unitable. This means that $s(p+q) = sp+sq$ is unitable, which is impossible by assumption. So, $q$ must be in $S\setminus\overline{U}$. 

Because these three properties hold, along with the fact that $0\in S\setminus\overline{U}$ and the standard associativity still holds, we have that $S\setminus\overline{U}$ is a $k$-ideal of $S$. 

[b]Alternate approaches: [/b]

My analysis of this problem so far has not really used the fact that $S$ is Goldbach. Any work I have done in the past utilizing the assumption that $S$ is Goldbach and not utilizing the Kaplan-X approach of subtracting out units hasn't shown any results for polynomials like $$(p+p)x^{s_0} + a_1x^{s_1} + \ldots + a_kx^{s_k} + (p+p)$$ or $$(p+p)x^{s_0} + a_1x^{s_1} + \ldots + a_kx^{s_k} + (p+p).$$ I'm discouraged from considering conditions like ACCP since even the presence of one non-trivial $k$-ideal is enough to make a semidomain not satisfy condition $C'$ (from the paper linked above). I don't know what imposing additional restrictions on $S$, like forcing it to be a UFS/HFS/BFS will do to help solve the problem.

posts.title: Open Problem 2
posts.text:
We will prove Goldbach ascent for certain semidomains $S$ in this and the following four posts. This post will provide key definitions, conditions, and other information to be referenced later.  

[b]Definition: Goldbach semidomain[/b]
A semidomain $S$ is said to be [i]Goldbach[/i] if for every $s\in S$, $2s$ is either a unit, an irreducible, or the sum of two irreducibles. 

[b]Condition $\star$: [/b]
A semidomain $S$ is said to satisfy $(\star)$ if every irreducible $p\in S$ may be expressed as the sum $a+b$, where $a, b\in S$ share no common nonunit factors. 

Consider $$f=\sum_{i=0}^n s_ix^{k_i}\in S[x^{\pm 1}]$$ where $s_i\in S$ and $k_i\in \mathbb{Z}$ for all $0\leq i\leq n$. Additionally, $k_i > k_{i+1}$ for $0\leq i < n$. We wish to show that $2f$ is a unit, irreducible, or the sum of two irreducibles. To do this, we employ an approach similar to the one used by Kaplan and X in [url]https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.14888[/url]. It is necessary to consider the leading/trailing coefficients of $2f$, namely $2s_0$ and $2s_n$. So, we let $(2s_0, 2s_n)$ represent a polynomial with leading coefficient $2s_0$ and trailing coefficient $2s_n$. 

Note that if $S$ is Goldbach, then every element $2s$ for $s\in S$ is either a unit $u$, an irreducible $p$, or the sum of two irreducibles $p+q$. So, there are $18$ cases for the leading and trailing coefficients of a polynomial $f\in S[x^{\pm 1}]$ for a Goldbach semidomain $S$: 

1. $(u, u)$
2. $(u, p)$
3. $(p, p)$
4. $(p, q)$
5. $(u, p+p)$
6. $(u, p+q)$
7. $(p, p+p)$
8. $(p, p+q)$
9. $(p, q+r)$
10. $(p, q+q)$
11. $(p+p, p+p)$
12. $(p+p, p+q)$
13. $(p+p, q+q)$
14. $(p+p, q+r)$
15. $(p+q, r+r)$
16. $(p+q, p+q)$
17. $(p+q, p+r)$
18. $(p+q, r+s)$

Moving forward, we take $S$ to be an additively reduced and semisubtractive (but not necessarily Goldbach) semidomain. Furthermore, $p, q, r, s \in S$ are non-associate irreducibles, while $u, v\in S^\times$ are units. 

As a remark, note that condition $(\star)$ always holds in such semidomains $S$ unless some irreducible $p$ is only additively divisible by associates of $p$. Also note that at most one irreducible may disrupt $(\star)$ in this way as for two irreducibles $p, q\in S$, either $p-q$ or $q-p$ must also be in $S$.

posts.title: Open Problem 2
posts.text:
[b]Case $1$: $S$ is also not antimatter[/b]

Since $S$ is semisubtractive, only one atom can exist. If this atom is not a unit, it is well known that $S[x^{\pm 1}]$ is not Goldbach. 

Otherwise, say that the atom is some unit $u$. Then, for every $s\in S\setminus\{0\}$, $s-u$ must be in $S$ since otherwise $u=(u-s)+s$ would not be an atom. By Theorem $3.6$ of [url]https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.00590[/url], this means that $S[x^{\pm 1}]$ is Goldbach.

posts.title: Open Problem 2
posts.text:
[b]Case $2.1$: $S$ is also antimatter and $2$ is an irreducible element[/b]

Since $2$ is irreducible, it is impossible for $2s$ to be a unit for $s\in S$. So, cases $1$, $2$, $5$, and $6$ are impossible. Also, since $2$ is irreducible, $2s_0=p$ implies that $p$ is an associate of $2$. It is important to note that $p=2u$ implies $p=(1+1)u=u+u$. A similar result is true in the case of $2s_n=p$. 

These results allow us to resolve all cases for polynomials with at least $4$ terms if $(\star)$ holds: 

1. $(u, u)$ --- does not exist
2. $(u, p)$ --- does not exist
3. $(p, p)$ --- $(u, u)+(u, u)$
4. $(p, q)$ --- $(u, a)+(u, b)$
5. $(u, p+p)$ --- does not exist
6. $(u, p+q)$ --- does not exist
7. $(p, p+p)$ --- $(u, p)+(u, p)$
8. $(p, p+q)$ --- $(u, p)+(u, q)$
9. $(p, q+r)$ --- $(u, q)+(u, r)$
10. $(p, q+q)$ --- $(u, q)+(u, q)$
11. $(p+p, p+p)$ --- $(a, p+a)+(p+b, b)$; requires $(\star)$
12. $(p+p, p+q)$ --- either $(p+a, p)+(b, q)$ or $(p+b, p)+(a, q)$ depending on which of $a$ and $b$ is coprime to $q$. Note that both $a$ and $b$ cannot share factors with $q$, as the irreducibility of $q$ implies that $q\mid a+b$, which is impossible for non-associate irreducibles $p$ and $q$. Also requires $(\star)$. 
13. $(p+p, q+q)$ --- $(p, q)+(p, q)$
14. $(p+p, q+r)$ --- $(p, q)+(p, r)$
15. $(p+q, r+r)$ --- $(p, r)+(q, r)$
16. $(p+q, p+q)$ --- $(p, q)+(q, p)$
17. $(p+q, p+r)$ --- $(p, r)+(q, p)$
18. $(p+q, r+s)$ --- $(p, r)+(q, s)$

These decompositions also prove Goldbach for polynomials with $2$ terms. This is because all binomials are monolithic, so if the coefficients of a binomial share no nonunit factors, then the binomial is irreducible.

posts.title: Open Problem 2
posts.text:
[b]Case $2.2$: $S$ is also antimatter and $2$ is a unit[/b]

Since $2$ is a unit, it follows by the definition of the Goldbach property that every element of $S$ is either a unit, an irreducible, or the sum of two irreducibles. As such, all $18$ cases listed above are possible. To prove this case, a few observations are necessary. 

[b]Lemma: [/b]
For every unit $u\in S^\times$, there exists $v\in S^\times$ such  that $u-v\in S$. 

[b]Proof: [/b]
Assume for contradiction that there exists $u\in S^\times$ such that $u-v\notin S$ for any $v\in S^\times\setminus\{u\}$ (for such a $u$, suitable $v$ must exist since there is more than $1$ unit in $S$). Since $S$ is semisubtractive, there can only exist one such $u$. Semisubtractivity also implies that $v-u\in S$ and that either $uv-v^{-1}\in S$ or $v^{-1}-uv\in S$ for all $v\in S^\times\setminus\{u\}$. If $uv-v^{-1}\in S$, then $(v^{-1}-u)(uv+u)+(uv-v^{-1})u = u - u^2\in S$. Otherwise, if $v^{-1}-uv\in S$, then $(uv-u)(v^{-1}+u)+(v^{-1}-uv)u=u-u^2\in S$. Either way, if $u\neq u^2$, this is a contradiction. 

On the other hand, if $u=u^2$, we must have $u=1$. However, note that $1-2^{-1}$ must be in $S$ since otherwise $2\cdot 2(2^{-1}+1)(2^{-1}-1)=1-4\in S$ due to semisubtractivity, which is clearly impossible. So, $u=1$ also yields a contradiction. [b]End of proof[/b]

Furthermore, for $t\in S$, note that $2t=u$ implies that $u=t+t$, where $t$ is also a unit. Similarly, $2t=p$ implies that $p=t+t$ where $t$ is an irreducible. So, we can ignore cases with a single irreducible as the leading/trailing coefficient. 

We also require that $(\star)$ holds. If this is true, we can prove that Goldbach holds for all polynomials with $2$ (see reasoning in the post above) or at least $4$ terms. In accordance with $(\star)$, we will express $p=a+b$ where $a$ and $b$ share no common nonunit factors. 

1. $(u, u)$ --- $(t, t)+(t, t)$ for $t\in S$ such that $2t=u$. 
2. $(u, p)$ --- ignored (same as case $5$)
3. $(p, p)$ --- ignored (same as case $11$)
4. $(p, q)$ --- ignored (same as case $13$)
5. $(u, p+p)$ --- $(t, p)+(t, p)$ for $t\in S$ such that $2t=u$. 
6. $(u, p+q)$ --- $(t, p)+(t, q)$ for $t\in S$ such that $2t=u$. 
7. $(p, p+p)$ --- ignored (same as case $11$)
8. $(p, p+q)$ --- ignored (same as case $12$)
9. $(p, q+r)$ --- ignored (same as case $14$)
10. $(p, q+q)$ --- $(u, q)+(u, q)$
11. $(p+p, p+p)$ --- $(a, p+a)+(p+b, b)$
12. $(p+p, p+q)$ --- either $(p+a, p)+(b, q)$ or $(p+b, p)+(a, q)$ depending on which of $a$ and $b$ is coprime to $q$. Note that both $a$ and $b$ cannot share factors with $q$, as the irreducibility of $q$ implies that $q\mid a+b$, which is impossible for non-associate irreducibles $p$ and $q$. 
13. $(p+p, q+q)$ --- $(p, q)+(p, q)$
14. $(p+p, q+r)$ --- $(p, q)+(p, r)$
15. $(p+q, r+r)$ --- $(p, r)+(q, r)$
16. $(p+q, p+q)$ --- $(p, q)+(q, p)$
17. $(p+q, p+r)$ --- $(p, r)+(q, p)$
18. $(p+q, r+s)$ --- $(p, r)+(q, s)$

posts.title: Open Problem 3.1
posts.text:
[b]Theorem 1.[/b] Let $f \in \mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. If $f$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$, then $f$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. Consequently
\[
\mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]] \cap \mathcal{A}(\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]) \subseteq \mathcal{A}(\mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]).
\]
[i]Proof.[/i] Let $f \in \mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]$ be an irreducible element of $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. Assume, towards a contradiction, that $f$ is reducible in $\mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. Then there exist nonunits $g, h \in \mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]$ such that $f=gh$. Because $\mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]$ is a subsemiring of $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$, the factorization $f=gh$ also holds in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$.

By virtue of the irreducibility of $f$ in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$, either $g$ or $h$ must be a unit in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. Without loss of generality, assume $g$ is a unit in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. As all coefficients of $g$ belong to $\mathbb{N}_0$, its LD coefficient must be $1$, then, $g$ is a unit in $\mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. This contradicts the assumption that $g$ is a nonunit in $\mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. Therefore, $f$ must be irreducible in $\mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. $\square$

The reverse inclusion of Theorem 1 does not hold; the following proposition provides an infinite family of such counterexamples.

[b]Proposition 2.[/b] For any integer $k \ge 1$, the polynomial $f_k(x)=x^4+4k^4$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]$ but is reducible in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$.

[i]Proof.[/i] The reducibility of $f_k(x)$ in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$ follows from the Sophie Germain identity
\[
x^4+4k^4 = (x^2+2kx+2k^2)(x^2-2kx+2k^2).
\]
Let $g(x) = x^2+2kx+2k^2$ and $h(x) = x^2-2kx+2k^2$. The LD coefficient of both factors is $2k^2$. Since $k \ge 1$, we have $2k^2 \neq \pm 1$, which ensures that neither $g(x)$ nor $h(x)$ is a unit in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. Thus, $f_k(x)$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$.

We proceed to argue that $f_k(x)$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. Because $f_k(x)$ is a polynomial with nonnegative coefficients, any factorization $f_k=gh$ in $\mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]$ requires that both $g$ and $h$ must be polynomials in $\mathbb{N}_0[x]$. Such a factorization is also valid in the polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z}[x]$. The ring $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a UFD, where the irreducible factors of $f_k(x)$ are $x^2+2kx+2k^2$ and $x^2-2kx+2k^2$. The second of these factors is not in $\mathbb{N}_0[x]$ as the coefficient of $x$ is $-2k < 0$. Therefore, no factorization of $f_k(x)$ into two nonunits exists within $\mathbb{N}_0[x]$, which implies that $f_k(x)$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. $\square$

[b]Proposition 3.[/b] The monomial atoms of $\mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]$, which are of the form $px^k$ for a prime integer $p$ and $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, are also irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$.

[i]Proof.[/i] Let $f=px^k$. Assume, towards a contradiction, that $f=gh$ for some nonunits $g, h \in \mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. Let $v \colon \mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]] \setminus \{0\} \to \mathbb{Z}$ be the valuation map, which sends a series to the exponent of its LD term. It is clear that $v(gh) = v(g)+v(h)$. For the series $f=px^k$, we have $v(f)=k$, so $k = v(g)+v(h)$.

Let $g_0$ and $h_0$ be the coefficients of the LD terms of $g$ and $h$, respectively. The coefficient of the LD term of the product $gh$ is $g_0 h_0$. For the series $f$, this coefficient is $p$. This gives the integer equation $p = g_0 h_0$. Because $p$ is a prime integer, its only integer factors are $\pm 1$ and $\pm p$. This implies that either $g_0 \in \{\pm 1\}$ or $h_0 \in \{\pm 1\}$. If $g_0 \in \{\pm 1\}$, then $g$ is a unit in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. If $h_0 \in \{\pm 1\}$, then $h$ is a unit in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. In either case, we find a contradiction to the assumption that both $g$ and $h$ were nonunits. Hence, $f$ must be irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. $\square$

[b]Example 4.[/b] Polynomials in $\mathbb{N}_0[x]$ that are irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ and are not units in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$ lie in the intersection $\mathcal{A}(\mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]) \cap \mathcal{A}(\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]])$.

A polynomial $f(x) \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a unit in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$ if and only if its LD nonzero coefficient is $\pm 1$. If an irreducible polynomial in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ does not satisfy this condition, it remains irreducible as a formal Laurent series in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. By virtue of Theorem 1, it is then also irreducible in $\mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. This provides large families of common irreducibles. For example, if $f(x) \in \mathbb{N}_0[x]$ satisfies Eisenstein's criterion for some prime $p$, then it is irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$. The criterion requires the LD coefficient to be divisible by $p$ but not by $p^2$, which ensures this coefficient is not $\pm 1$. Thus, $f(x)$ is not a unit in $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$. It is therefore irreducible in both $\mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]]$ and $\mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]]$.

posts.title: Open Problem 3.1
posts.text:
Let \( f(x) \in \mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]] \) or \( \mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]] \) be a non-zero Laurent series. We may write
\[
f(x) = x^{\mathrm{ord}(f)} \sum_{i=0}^\infty a_{\mathrm{ord}(f)+i} x^i.
\]
Let \( N_f = \mathrm{ord}(f) \). Define the associated power series
\[
\tilde{f}(x) = x^{-N_f} f(x) = \sum_{i=0}^\infty a_{N_f+i} x^i,
\]
so that \( \tilde{f}(0) = a_{N_f} \neq 0 \). Suppose \( f(x) \) is a unit. Then there exists \( g(x) \) such that \( f(x)g(x) = 1 \), and we can similarly write \( g(x) = x^{N_g} \tilde{g}(x) \) with \( \tilde{g}(0) \neq 0 \). The product becomes
\[
f(x)g(x) = x^{N_f + N_g} \tilde{f}(x)\tilde{g}(x) = 1,
\]
implying \( N_f + N_g = 0 \) and \( \tilde{f}(x)\tilde{g}(x) = 1 \). Let \( \tilde{f}(x) = \sum_{i=0}^\infty b_i x^i \), \( \tilde{g}(x) = \sum_{j=0}^\infty c_j x^j \). Then \( b_0 c_0 = 1 \).

In \( \mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]] \), the coefficients \( b_i, c_j \in \mathbb{N}_0 \), so the only solution to \( b_0 c_0 = 1 \) is \( b_0 = c_0 = 1 \). The product \( \tilde{f}(x)\tilde{g}(x) = 1 \) then implies \( b_1 + c_1 = 0 \), so \( b_1 = c_1 = 0 \), and by induction, all higher \( b_i = c_i = 0 \). Hence \( \tilde{f}(x) = 1 \), so \( f(x) = x^{N_f} \). The units are exactly the monomials \( \{x^k : k \in \mathbb{Z}\} \).

In \( \mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]] \), the coefficients lie in \( \mathbb{Z} \), so \( b_0 c_0 = 1 \) implies \( b_0 = \pm 1 \). But for \( \tilde{f}(x)\tilde{g}(x) = 1 \) to hold with power series over \( \mathbb{Z} \), the constant term must be a unit in \( \mathbb{Z} \), i.e., \( \pm 1 \), and the higher coefficients must vanish ��� otherwise \( \tilde{g}(x) \) becomes an infinite series with nonzero coefficients, and the product is not 1. Hence \( \tilde{f}(x) = \pm 1 \) and \( f(x) = \pm x^k \). The units are exactly \( \{\pm x^k : k \in \mathbb{Z}\} \).

Suppose \( f \in \mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]] \) is irreducible in \( \mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]] \). Then \( f \) is not a unit in \( \mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]] \), so \( f \neq \pm x^k \), and since \( f \in \mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]] \), we also have \( f \neq -x^k \). Therefore, \( f \) is not a unit in \( \mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]] \) either. Suppose \( f = gh \) with \( g, h \in \mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]] \). Then the same factorization holds in \( \mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]] \), contradicting the irreducibility of \( f \) unless one factor is a unit in \( \mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]] \), i.e., \( \pm x^k \). But since \( g, h \in \mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]] \), the only such units possible are \( x^k \in \mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]] \), which are also units in \( \mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]] \). So \( f \) is irreducible in \( \mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]] \).

Now consider the polynomial \( f(x) = x^4 + 4 \). First, this is not a unit in either ring. Suppose \( f(x) = G(x)H(x) \) with \( G(x), H(x) \in \mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]] \). Since \( f(x) \) is a polynomial, so must \( G(x) \) and \( H(x) \). Because \( \mathrm{ord}(f) = 0 \), we must have \( \mathrm{ord}(G) = \mathrm{ord}(H) = 0 \), so \( G(x), H(x) \in \mathbb{N}_0[x] \). Then \( f(x) = G(x)H(x) \) also holds in \( \mathbb{Z}[x] \). Using the Sophie Germain identity,
\[
x^4 + 4 = (x^2 + 2x + 2)(x^2 - 2x + 2),
\]
we note that both factors are irreducible in \( \mathbb{Z}[x] \). However, \( x^2 - 2x + 2 \notin \mathbb{N}_0[x] \), so it cannot be a factor in \( \mathbb{N}_0[x] \). Thus \( x^4 + 4 \) is irreducible in \( \mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]] \), but reducible in \( \mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]] \).

Therefore, irreducibility in \( \mathbb{Z}[[\mathbb{Z}]] \) implies irreducibility in \( \mathbb{N}_0[[\mathbb{Z}]] \), but not conversely.

posts.title: Open Problem 3.1
posts.text:
@user Thanks for pointing that out. I have revised the proof and I think it avoids these mistakes. Please let me know if there are any more flaws. I'm fairly confident the theorem is true, since I have tested by code.

[b]Lemma[/b] Every nonunit irreducible in the semiring $\mathbb N_0[[\mathbb Z]]$ has finite support and, up to multiplication by a monomial $x^k$, can be written $f(x)=x^m\,p(x), p(x)=\sum_{i=0}^d c_i\,x^i\in\mathbb Z[x], c_0=1,\;d\ge1,$
and its coefficients $(c_0,\dots,c_d)$ satisfy exactly one of
1. all $c_i\ge0$,
2. there exist $i,j$ with $c_i>0>c_j$.

[b]Proof[/b] In $\mathbb N_0[[\mathbb Z]]$, any product of two series each having at least two nonzero terms itself has at least two nonzero terms.  Hence the only way $u\cdot v=1$ can hold is if one of $u,v$ has exactly one term $x^k$ and coefficient $1$.  Thus the units are precisely the monomials $x^k$. If $f(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}c_nx^n$ has infinitely many nonzero $c_n$ for $n\ge N$, split it as $f(x) =\Bigl(\sum_{n< N}c_nx^n\Bigr) \cdot \Bigl(\sum_{m\ge0}d_mx^m\Bigr),$ where the nonnegative $d_m$ are chosen by matching coefficients.  Neither factor is a monomial (each has a nonzero constant term and at least one higher degree term), so this is a nontrivial factorization in the semiring.  A similar argument handles infinitely many nonzeros for $n\le M$.  Thus any irreducible has only finitely many nonzero coefficients.

After dividing out the monomial unit, write $f(x)=x^m p(x)$ with $p(x)=\sum_{i=0}^d c_i x^i$ and $c_0=1>0$.  Then either every $c_i\ge0$, or else some $c_j<0$, in which case $c_0>0$ forces some $c_i>0$.  The two cases are clearly disjoint and exhaustive.

[b]Theorem.[/b] Let $f(x)\in\mathbb Z[[\mathbb Z]]$ be irreducible in the ring and satisfy $f(0)=\pm1$.  Write $f(x)=x^m\sum_{i=0}^d c_i\,x^i,\qquad c_0=1.$ Then $f$ remains irreducible in the semiring $\mathbb N_0[[\mathbb Z]]$ if and only if its coefficient sequence satisfies exactly one of
a) all $c_i\ge0$, 
b) there exist $i,j$ with $c_i>0>c_j$.

[b]Proof.[/b] By the Lemma we reduce to the finite polynomial $p(x)=\sum_{i=0}^d c_i x^i$.

$(\Rightarrow)$ 
If $f$ remains irreducible in the semiring, then either $p$ has all $c_i\ge0$ or mixed signs, by the Lemma.

$(\Leftarrow)$
- If all $c_i\ge0$, then any factorization $p=G\cdot H$ in $\mathbb N_0[x]$ would lift to a factorization in $\mathbb Z[x]$ (coefficients unchanged), contradicting  that $f$ (hence $p$) is irreducible in the ring.
- If there exist $i,j$ with $c_i>0>c_j$, then any would���be factorization $p=G\cdot H$ in $\mathbb N_0[[\mathbb Z]]$ with 
  $G=\sum g_r x^r,\;H=\sum h_s x^s$ would produce $[x^j]\,p=\sum_{r+s=j}g_r\,h_s \ge0,$ contradicting $c_j<0$.  So no nontrivial semiring factorization exists.

posts.title: Proof of Conjecture 4.5, and Counterexample to Open Problem 2
posts.text:
So apparently, I am terrible at using aops and did not discover the existence of the message board, along with all of the existing content, until after I wrote this proof. Therefore, sorry if I repeat any content that has already been proven.

In resources, Goldbach semidomains are defined as follows: An additively reduced semidomain $S$ is called a Goldbach semidomain if $2s$ can be written as the sum of two (multiplicative) irreducibles for every $s \in S^* \setminus S^\times$. I assume that this definition avoids integers up to units (which I will call monomials in my writing), as otherwise, this problem becomes equivalent to the actual Goldbach conjecture and thus would be way beyond of our scope.

I did not see the resources before writing my proof. In my writing, I had defined Goldbach semidomains instead as such: An additively reduced, additively non-antimatter, and multiplicatively non-antimatter semidomain $S$ is called a Goldbach semidomain if every non-monomial $s \in S$ with $\max(\mathsf{L}_{S^+}(s)) > 3$ can be written as the sum of exactly two elements of $\mathcal{A}_\times(S)$. In essence, for any element, if it can be expressed as a sum of four or more additive atoms, then it is the sum of exactly two irreducibles.

I claim that, throughout my proof, the second definition always encompasses the first definition. In the first section of my proof, I assume $\mathcal{A}_+(S) = S^\times$, and therefore, $\max(\mathsf{L}_{S^+}(2s)) \geq 4$ for all $s \in S^* \setminus S^\times$, so this is fine.

In the second section of my proof, where I give the counterexample, the above is no longer the case, and instead $S^\times \subset \mathcal{A}_+(S)$. Therefore, in order to reconcile the two definitions, we must consider the edge case where we write $2f$ as a sum of two irreducibles when $f \in \mathcal{A}_+(S) \setminus S^\times$. However, for the specific semidomain $S$ that I had, I showed that every $f \in \mathcal{A}_+(S) \setminus S^\times$ must satisfy $\ell(f - 1 - x^d) = 0$, which allows us to apply Lemma 2.3 (from my proof) and conclude that any such $f$ must be an irreducible. Therefore, $2f$ can be written as $f + f$ in this case. All other cases require $f \in S^* \setminus \mathcal{A}_+(S)$ and are thus covered by $\max(\mathsf{L}_{S^+}(2f)) \geq 4$; therefore, the proof I provided (using the second definition) is strictly stronger than the first definition of a Goldbach semidomain, and is hence valid.


I prove two main things:
1) Conjecture 4.5 from [url=https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.14888]Kaplan X 2023[/url] is true, and a corollary is that strong Goldbach holds in the Laurent power series extension of $\mathbb{N}_0$ (I believe this was unsolved prior to this writing).
2) The weird semidomain $S = \mathbb{N}_0[x^{\pm 1}; 1 + q(x) + x^k \mid k \in \mathbb{N}, q(x) \in \mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}[x], \deg(q) \leq k]$ is an additively reduced, additively atomic, and Goldbach semidomain which satisfies $\mathcal{A}_+(S) \neq S^\times$. By Conjecture 4.5 (or Theorem 4.4 from the linked paper, it is a weaker version but still plenty enough for this implication), it follows that the Laurent polynomial/series extensions of $S$ (these would be $S[y^{\pm 1}]$ and $S[[y^{\pm 1}]]$) cannot be Goldbach semidomains.

I have attached the proof as a pdf. There may be errors, hopefully none significant enough to nullify the result. I would greatly appreciate any feedback.

posts.text:
[quote=]I do not think it is valid to just ignore monomials.[/quote]

Thank you for your question. Could I ask how we can determine the Goldbach property in many semidomains which have been well-established to be Goldbach semidomains?

For example, $\mathbb{N}_0[x^{\pm 1}]$ was proven to be a Goldbach semidomain by [url=https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.01189]Liao and X[/url] in 2023. One of the key conditions provided is that $|\mathsf{supp}(f)| > 1$, i.e., $f$ is not a monomial. Indeed, we know that any integer $n \in \mathbb{N}_0[x^{\pm 1}]$ can only be written as a sum of other integers. Therefore, if we are to include monomials in our definition, it follows that proving the Goldbach property is at least as difficult as proving the Goldbach conjecture; this is intractable.

To be safe, you can confirm this with one of the mentors, but I'm pretty sure that it is standard practice to only consider non-monomials, since I've discussed this topic with X before.

posts.title: Open Problem 4.2
posts.text:
If $S[x^{\pm 1}]$ is strong Goldbach then $G(S)[x^{\pm 1}]$ is also strong Goldbach. 

[b]Proof[/b]: 

Take $f\in G(S)[x^{\pm 1}]$. If $f\in S[x^{\pm 1}]$, then $f$ is the sum of two irreducibles in $S[x^{\pm 1}]$. Since irreducibles in $S[x^{\pm 1}]$ are also irreducible in $G(S)[x^{\pm 1}]$, $f$ satisfies the strong Goldbach property. 

Otherwise, $f=-g$ for some $g\in S[x^{\pm 1}]$. We know $g=p+q$ for irreducibles $p, q\in S[x^{\pm 1}]$, so $f = (-p) + (-q)$, where $-p$ and $-q$ are in $G(S)[x^{\pm 1}]$. Since $-1$ is a unit of $G(S)$, $-p$ and $-q$ are still irreducible in $G(S)[x^{\pm 1}]$. 

------------------------

Now, assume the converse: $G(S)[x^{\pm 1}]$ is strong Goldbach. We may express $f\in S[x^{\pm 1}]$ as the sum of irreducibles $p$ and $q$ in $G(S)[x^{\pm 1}]$. If $p$ and $q$ are both in $S$, we are done. 

Otherwise, note that it is impossible for both $p$ and $q$ to not be in $S[x^{\pm 1}]$ since otherwise $-p, -q\in S[x^{\pm 1}]$ which implies $-p-q=-f\in S[x^{\pm 1}]$, contradicting the fact that $S$ is additively reduced. 

So, the only other possibility is for, WLOG, $p\in S[x^{\pm 1}]$ and $-q\in S[x^{\pm 1}]$.

posts.title: Open Problem 0
posts.text:
I've been trying some simple cases to help me get an intuitive understanding of the problem.

The cases I'm exploring are where you have a pair $(q_1, q_2)$ with $q_2 = q_1^{-1}$.

The simplest such pair I could think about is the pair $(p, p^{-1})$, where $p$ is a prime number.

Here's what I found:
[b]Proposition[/b]
The finitely generated Puiseux semiring $\mathbb{N}_0[p, p^{-1}]$, where $p \in \mathbb{P}_{\geq 5}$ is Goldbach-like with a bound $M \leq 16$.

[b]Proof[/b]

These theorems will be used in this proof.

[b]Theorem (Helfgott, 2013)[/b]
[i]Every odd number greater than 5 can be expressed as the sum of three primes (repetitions allowed).
[/i]
[b]Corollary. [/b]
[i]Every $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$ can be written as a sum of at most four primes.[/i]

Let
$$
S= \mathbb{N}_0[p, p^{-1}] = 
\left\{ \sum_{i=0}^{m} \sum_{j=0}^{n} a_{ij} p^i p^{-j}
\;\middle|\; m,n \in \mathbb{N}_0,\; a_{ij} \in \mathbb{N}_0, p \in \mathbb{P}_{\geq 5} \right\}
$$
$$
= \left\{ \sum_{i=0}^{m} \sum_{j=0}^{n} \frac{a_{ij} p^i}{p^j}
\;\middle|\; m,n \in \mathbb{N}_0,\; a_{ij} \in \mathbb{N}_0, p \in \mathbb{P}_{\geq 5} \right\}
$$
$$
= \left\{\frac{n}{p^k}
\;\middle|\; n, k \in \mathbb{N}_0, p \in \mathbb{P}_{\geq 5} \right\}
$$
$$S^* = \left\{\frac{n}{p^k}
\;\middle|\; n, k \in \mathbb{N}, p \in \mathbb{P}_{\geq 5} \right\}$$

[b]Group of Units[/b]
The group of units of units of $S^*$ is $\left\{ p^z \; \middle|\; p \in \mathbb{P}_{\geq 5}, z \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}$

Proof

For an element $\frac{n}{p^k} \in S^*$ to be invertible, there has to be an element $x \in S^*$ such that $\frac{n}{p^k} \cdot x = 1$.
For that to be possible $x$ has to be equal to $\frac{p^k}{n}$.
But for $\frac{p^k}{n}$ to be in $S^*$, $n$ has to be be a power of $p$. 
Let $n = p^m$ with $m \in \mathbb{N}_0$.
We have:
$\frac{n}{p^k} \cdot x = \frac{p^m}{p^k} \cdot \frac{p^k}{p^m} = 1$

So for $\frac{n}{p^k}$ to be invertible implies that is equal to $\frac{p^m}{p^k}$.
$\frac{p^m}{p^k} = p^{m-k} = p^z$ with $z \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $z = m-k$.

Let $u = p^z$ where $z \in \mathbb{Z}$. We must show $u^{-1} = p^{-z} \in S^*$.

- If $z \ge 0$, we have:
    $$u^{-1} = p^{-z} = \frac{1}{p^z}$$
    Since $1 \in \mathbb{N}$ and $z \in \mathbb{N}_0$, $u^{-1} \in S^*$.

- If $z < 0$:
	Let $z = -k$, with $k$ a negative integer.
    $$u^{-1} = p^{-z} = p^{-(-k)} = p^k = \frac{p^k}{1} = \frac{p^k}{p^0}$$
    Since $p^k \in \mathbb{N}$ and $1 = p^0$, $u^{-1} \in S^*$.

In both cases, $u^{-1} \in S^*$. 

Therefore,
$$S^{\times} = \left\{ p^z \; \middle|\; p \in \mathbb{P}_{\geq 5}, z \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}$$ $\square$

[b]Set of Multiplicative Irreducible[/b]
The set of multiplicative irreducible of $S$ is $\Big\{ \frac{r}{p^k}, r \in \mathbb{P} \setminus \{p \}, k \in \mathbb{N}_0 \Big\}$.

Proof

Take any $\frac{n}{p^k}$ in $S^*$ (to exclude 0)

$n$ can always be written as $p^t \cdot m$, with $t \in \mathbb{N}_0, m \in \mathbb{N}$ and $gcd(p, m) = 1$.

Write $\frac{n}{p^k}$ as $\frac{p^t \cdot m}{p^k} = p^{t-k} \cdot m$

If $m = 1$ then $\frac{n}{p^k}$ will be equal to $p^{t-k} \cdot 1$, which is a unit, hence not irreducible.

If $m$ is composite then it has no prime factor that is equal to $p$ since $gcd(p, m) = 1$.
Write $m = r \cdot m^{\prime}$, with $r \in \mathbb{P} \setminus \{p\}, m^{\prime} \in \mathbb{N}$ and $m^{\prime} \geq 2$.
Then $\frac{p^t \cdot m}{p^k} = \frac{p^t \cdot (r \cdot m^{\prime})}{p^k} = \frac{r}{p^k} \cdot (p^t \cdot m^{\prime})$
which is a product of two non-unit, not  irreducible.

If $m$ is some prime $r \neq p$, 
We have
$\frac{p^t \cdot m}{p^k} = \frac{p^t \cdot r}{p^k}$
$= 1 \cdot (\frac{p^t \cdot r}{p^k})$
$= \frac{p^t}{p^k} \cdot r$
$= \frac{r}{p^k} \cdot p^t$
$= \frac{1}{p^k} \cdot rp^t$
in all those possible combinations, we always have a unit multiplied by a non unit.
Therefore $\frac{n}{p^k}$ being irreducible implies that $\frac{n}{p^k} = x = \frac{r}{p^k}$.

Let $x$ be an irreducible in $S^*$.

Assume $x$ is factored as a product of two elements $a, b \in S^{*}$:
$$x = a \cdot b$$

Let $a = \frac{n_a}{p^{k_a}}$ and $b = \frac{n_b}{p^{k_b}}$, where $n_a, n_b \in \mathbb{N}$ and $k_a, k_b \in \mathbb{N}_0$.

Substituting the fractional forms into the factorization:
$$\frac{r}{p^k} = \frac{n_a n_b}{p^{k_a+k_b}}$$

By comparing the numerators, we must have:
$$r = n_a n_b$$

Since $r$ is a prime number, its only factorization in the natural numbers is $1 \cdot r$. Therefore, we have only two possibilities for the numerators:
- Possibility 1: $n_a = 1$ and $n_b = r$
    The factor $a$ simplifies to:
    $$a = \frac{1}{p^{k_a}} = p^{-k_a}$$
    Since $p^{-k_a}$ is of the form $p^z$ with $z \in \mathbb{Z}$, $a$ is an element of the unit group: $a \in S^{\times}$.
- Possibility 2: $n_a = r$ and $n_b = 1$
    The factor $b$ simplifies to:
    $$b = \frac{1}{p^{k_b}} = p^{-k_b}$$
    Thus, $b \in S^{\times}$.

Since every possible factorization $x = a \cdot b$ forces at least one of the factors ($a$ or $b$) to be a unit, $x$ cannot be factored into two non-units.

Therefore for all element $\frac{n}{p^k} \in S^*, \frac{n}{p^k}$ is irreducible iff $n = r$, with $r \in \mathbb{P} \setminus \{p\}$

$\square$

[b]Proving that it's Goldbach-like:[/b]

Let's pick $\frac{n}{p^k}$ in $S^* \setminus S^{\times}$.

By the corollary of Helfgott theorem,
$$\frac{n}{p^k} = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{q_i}{p^k}$$
with $q_i \in \mathbb{P}, m \in \mathbb{N}$ and $m <= 4$.

But there can be a case where one or more of the $q_i$ is equal to $p$, that's a case we want to avoid.
Example:
$\frac{17}{5} = \frac{2}{5} + \frac{3}{5} + \frac{5}{5} + \frac{7}{5}$
Here $\frac{5}{5}$ is not irreducible.

To avoid it we will do replacements.

If $p = 5$ and one or more of the $q_i$ is equal to $p$ . For each $q_i = p = 5$ write
$5 = 2 + 3$.

If $p = 7$ and one or more of the $q_i$ is equal to $p$ . For each $q_i = p = 7$ write
$7 = 2 + 5$.

If $p \geq 11$ and one or more of the $q_i$ is equal to $p$. For each $q_i = p$, write 
$q = 2 + (q - 2)$

Since $q$ is odd, $q-2$ is also odd and $q -2 \geq 9$.

By Helfgott theorem $q - 2$  can be expressed as the sum of three primes with repetitions allowed.

So $q = 2 + s_1 + s_2 + s_3$, with $s_i \in \mathbb{P}$.

That means our replacement produce 4 primes different than $q$ (since they have to add up to it) and different than $p$ (since $p$  is equal to $q$)

Now let's go back to this:
$$\frac{n}{p^k} = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{q_i}{p^k}$$

In the worst case scenario, we would have four $q_i$, each being equal to $p$, that would result in $4 \times 4 = 16$ primes in the numerator that are not equal to $p$.
That is:
$$\frac{n}{p^k} = \sum_{i=1}^M \frac{s_i}{p^k}$$
with $s_i \in \mathbb{P} \setminus \{ p \}, M \in \mathbb{N}$ and $M \leq 16$.

Therefore $\mathbb{N}_0[p,p^{-1}]$ where $p \in \mathbb{P}_{\geq 5}$ is Goldbach-like with a bound $M \leq 16$.

$\square$

[b]Note:[/b]
I think  $\mathbb{N}_0[2,2^{-1}]$ and  $\mathbb{N}_0[3,3^{-1}]$ are also Goldbach-like but proving the replacement schemes for the case where $q_i = p$ was taking me a lot of time so I decided to put them aside for now.

posts.text:
Thank you @user for the generalization ��� I think it moves us closer to a full solution.

I believe the conjecture you proposed, as currently stated, may not be accurate (or may be misstated). 

As written:

Let $Q=\{q_1, q_2\}$ be a pair of positive rational numbers. The Puiseux semiring $\mathbb{N}_0[Q]$ is Goldbach-like if and only if $q_1,q_2\ge 1$.

$\mathcal{P}_d(Q) = \{7, 11\}, \qquad \min(\mathcal{P}_d)=7\ge 5.$

$\mathbb{N}_0[Q] \text{ is Goldbach-like}.$

posts.title: Open Problem 0
posts.text:
@user
You are right, the two conjectures I proposed will not help us solve the problem, they will only help us move it by a needle.

Here is the thinking process:

Let $\mathcal{P}_d:=\mathcal{P}_d(\{\frac{a}{b}, \frac{c}{d}\})$ and let look at $\mathcal{P}_d$ in terms of its cardinality.

[b]-[/b] If $\left| \mathcal{P}_d \right| = 0$:
	$S$ is trivially Goldbach-like. 
	Since the denominators are both 1, each element in $S$ is of the form $\frac{n}{1}$, the set of units is $\{1\}$ and the irreducibles are the usual primes numbers. By the corollary of Helfgott theorem, every element in $S^* \setminus \{1\}$ can be written as a sum of at most 4 primes.

[b]-[/b] If $\left| \mathcal{P}_d \right| = 1$:
	. If $\mathcal{P}_d = \{2\}$, the first conjecture I proposed will help us.
	.  If $\mathcal{P}_d = \{3\}$, the second conjecture I proposed will help us.
	. If $\mathcal{P}_d = \{p, \text{with } p \text{ a prime number } \geq 5\}$, we've already proved this case. $S$ is Goldbach-like with a bound $M \leq 16$.

[b]-[/b] If $\left| \mathcal{P}_d \right| = 2$:
	. If $2, 3 \notin \mathcal{P}_d$, then $S$ is Goldbach-like because $\min(\mathcal{P}_d) \ge 5$.
	. If $2 \in \mathcal{P}_d$ but $3 \notin \mathcal{P}_d$, it's complicated. We have to show that every positive integer minus a finite set of exceptions can be written as a sum of primes from $\mathbb P\setminus\{2,p \mid \text{with p a prime} \neq 2\}$.
	. If $3 \in \mathcal{P}_d$ but $2 \notin \mathcal{P}_d$, like in the previous case, we have to show that every positive integer minus a finite set of exceptions can be written as a sum of primes from $\mathbb P\setminus\{3,p \mid \text{with p a prime} \neq 3\}$.
	. If $2, 3 \in \mathcal{P}_d$, we have to show that every positive integer minus a finite set of exceptions can be written as a sum of primes from $\mathbb P\setminus\{2, 3\}$.

[b]-[/b] If $\left| \mathcal{P}_d \right| \geq 3$:
	$2$ and $3$ are making things hard.

Maybe we need a different way of looking at the problem.

Do you know where we can find the proof of the result for $\mathbb{N}_0[q]$, the Crowdmath 2024 one.

problem_text:
Hi everyone!

We hope you are having a joyful break.

We just want to make sure you have interesting open problems to work in case you wish to do so during the break, and so we decided not only to released the open problems corresponding to Resource 3 a little earlier than Resource 3, but also release another open problem related to atomicity and the ACCP in the setting of finitely generated rational semirings.

Although you can find the three open problems in the Problem Tab as always, given that we have relabeled the original "Open Problem 1" as "Open Problem 2",  we have included the three open problems here.


[b]Open Problem 1:[/b]

(1a) Determine the $n$-tuples $(q_1, \dots, q_n) \in \mathbb{Q}^n$ such that the additive monoid of the rational semiring $S := \mathbb{N}_0[q_1, \dots, q_n]$ is atomic but does not satisfy the ACCP.
     
(1b) Determine the $n$-tuples $(q_1, \dots, q_n) \in \mathbb{Q}^n$ such that the multiplicative monoid $S^*$ of the rational semiring $S := \mathbb{N}_0[q_1, \dots, q_n]$ is atomic but does not satisfy the ACCP

[b]Open Problem 2:[/b] Let $S$ be a positive semiring. We say that $S$ is a [I]bi-half-factorial semiring[/i] (bi-HF semiring) if both the additive monoid $(S, +)$ and the multiplicative monoid $S^*$ are half-factorial monoids (HFM). On the other hand, we say that $S$ is a [I]bi-factorial semiring[/i] (bi-UF semiring) if both the additive monoid $(S, +)$ and the multiplicative monoid $S^*$ are unique factorization monoids (UFM).
    
We propose the following open problems, which are motivated by the Bi-UF Conjecture proposed by Baeth, Chapman, and X back in 2021.
     
(2a) Is every bi-HF rational semiring a bi-UF semiring?

(2b) Is $\mathbb{N}_0$ the only rational semiring that is a bi-HF semiring?

(2c) Is $\mathbb{N}_0$ the only rational semiring that is a bi-UF semiring?


[b]Open Problem 3[/b]. A semiring is called [i]additively reduced[/i] provided that its additive monoid is reduced. Let $S$ be an additively reduced semidomain, and let $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ with $\ell \ge 2$.

* We say that $S$ has the [i]weak $\ell$-Goldbach condition[/i] if there exists $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ and $r_1, \dots, r_k \in S$ such that every $s \in S \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^k r_iS^\times$ can be written as a sum of $m$ multiplicative atoms of $S$ for some positive integer $m$ with $1 \le m \le \ell$.

* We say that $S$ has the [i]$\ell$-Goldbach condition[/i] for some $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ if there exist $r_1, \dots, r_k \in S$ such that every $s \in S \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^k r_iS^\times$ can be written as a sum of exactly $\ell$ multiplicative atoms of $S$.

(3a) Determine the $n$-tuples $(q_1, \dots, q_n) \in \mathbb{Q}^n$ such that the semidomain $\mathbb{N}_0[q_1, \dots, q_n]$ satisfies the weak $\ell$-Goldbach condition for some $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$.

(3b) Determine the $n$-tuples $(q_1, \dots, q_n) \in \mathbb{Q}^n$ such that the semidomain $\mathbb{N}_0[q_1, \dots, q_n]$ satisfies the $\ell$-Goldbach condition for some $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$.


We are working on finishing Resource 3, and it will be uploaded soon!

Happy New Year!

Best,
The CrowdMath Team

posts.title: Open Problem 3a
posts.text:
Hi everyone, the open problem 3a is a generalization of the work we started [url=https://artofproblemsolving.com/polymath/mitprimes2025-2/f/c4514831h3693333_open_problem_0]a few months earlier [/url].
Since our past results had a hidden assumption about the numerators that could break the proofs, we propose a careful approach of looking at the set $\mathbb{N}_0[q_1, \dots, q_n]$.

Instead of assuming intuitively that the numerators will contain $\mathbb{N}$ for every possible denominator, we see the structure of the elements of the set as they are.


[b]Proposition 1:[/b]

Let $q_i = \frac{a_i}{b_i}$, $i=1,\dots,n$, with $a_i \in \mathbb{Z}$, $b_i \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\gcd(a_i, b_i) = 1$.
Then

$$\mathbb{N}_0[q_1, \dots, q_n] = \Bigg\{
\frac{\sum_{\alpha \in I} c_\alpha \Big(\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat{\alpha}_i - \alpha_i}\Big) \Big(\prod_{i=1}^n a_i^{\alpha_i}\Big)}{\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat{\alpha}_i}}
\;\Bigg|\; I \subset \mathbb{N}_0^n \text{ finite and nonempty}; \; c_\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0
\Bigg\}.
$$
where $\alpha = (\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n) \in I \; \text{and} \; \widehat{\alpha}_i := \max\{\alpha_i \mid \alpha = (\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)\in I\}$

Proof
By definition
$$\mathbb{N}_0[q_1, . . . , q_n ] := \Big\{ f(q_1, ..., q_n) : f \in \mathbb{N}_0[x_1, . . . , x_n ] \Big\}$$
so each element can be written as a finite sum
$$
\sum_{\alpha \in I} c_\alpha\, \frac{\Big(\prod_{i=1}^n a_i^{\alpha_i}\Big)}{\Big(\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\alpha_i}\Big)} 
\; \text{with} \; I \subset \mathbb{N}_0^n \text{ finite and nonempty}; \; c_\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0$$

For each $\alpha \in I$, the denominator of the corresponding term is $b_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots b_n^{\alpha_n}$.
By definition of $\widehat{\alpha}_i$, we have  $\alpha_i \leq \widehat{\alpha}_i$ for all $i$ and all $\alpha \in I$ .
Hence $\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\alpha_i} \mid \prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat{\alpha}_i}$.
Since this holds for every $\alpha \in I$ , the product $\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat{\alpha}_i}$ is divisible by the denominator of each term, and therefore it is a common denominator of the entire sum. 

Fix $x \in \mathbb{N}_0[q_1,\dots,q_n]$ 
$x = \sum_{\alpha \in I} c_\alpha\, \frac{\Big(\prod_{i=1}^n a_i^{\alpha_i}\Big)}{\Big(\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\alpha_i}\Big)}$
For each $\alpha \in I$ , define
$$x_\alpha := \frac{b_1^{\widehat{\alpha}_1} \cdots b_n^{\widehat{\alpha}_n}}{b_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots b_n^{\alpha_n}} = \prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat{\alpha}_i - \alpha_i} \in \mathbb{N}$$
Multiplying $x$ by $\frac{x_{\alpha}}{x_{\alpha}}$ yields
$$\sum_{\alpha \in I} c_\alpha\, \frac{x_{\alpha} \Big(\prod_{i=1}^n a_i^{\alpha_i}\Big)}{x_{\alpha} \Big(\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\alpha_i}\Big)}$$
$$= \sum_{\alpha \in I} c_\alpha\, \frac{\Big(\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat{\alpha}_i - \alpha_i}\Big) \Big(\prod_{i=1}^n a_i^{\alpha_i}\Big)}{\Big(\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat{\alpha}_i - \alpha_i}\Big) \Big(\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\alpha_i}\Big)}$$
$$= \sum_{\alpha \in I} c_\alpha\, \frac{\Big(\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat{\alpha}_i - \alpha_i}\Big) \Big(\prod_{i=1}^n a_i^{\alpha_i}\Big)}{\Big(\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat{\alpha}_i}\Big)}$$
$$= \frac{\sum_{\alpha \in I} c_\alpha \Big(\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat{\alpha}_i - \alpha_i}\Big) \Big(\prod_{i=1}^n a_i^{\alpha_i}\Big)}{\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat{\alpha}_i}}$$
Hence every $x \in \mathbb{N}_0[q_1,\dots,q_n]$ can be written as $\frac{\sum_{\alpha \in I} c_\alpha \Big(\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat{\alpha}_i - \alpha_i}\Big) \Big(\prod_{i=1}^n a_i^{\alpha_i}\Big)}{\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat{\alpha}_i}}$ for some index set $I$.
Therefore $$\mathbb{N}_0[q_1, \dots, q_n] = \Bigg\{
\frac{\sum_{\alpha \in I} c_\alpha \Big(\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat{\alpha}_i - \alpha_i}\Big) \Big(\prod_{i=1}^n a_i^{\alpha_i}\Big)}{\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat{\alpha}_i}}
\;\Bigg|\; I \subset \mathbb{N}_0^n \text{ finite and nonempty}; \; c_\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0
\Bigg\}.$$
 $\square$

[b]Proposition 2:[/b]

$\mathbb{N}_0[q_1, \dots, q_n]$ is additively reduced iff the $n$-tuples $(q_1, \dots, q_n) \in \mathbb{Q}^n_{\geq 0}$  

Proof

[b]I. $(q_1,\dots,q_n)\in\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}^n \Rightarrow \mathbb{N}_0[q_1,\dots,q_n]$ is additively reduced[/b]

By Proposition 1 every element of $S:=\mathbb{N}_0[q_1,\dots,q_n]$ can be written in the form $$ \frac{N}{B},\qquad B=\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat\alpha_i},\quad N=\sum_{\alpha\in I} c_\alpha\Big(\prod_{i=1}^n b_i^{\widehat\alpha_i-\alpha_i}\Big)\Big(\prod_{i=1}^n a_i^{\alpha_i}\Big), $$ with $c_\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_0$. If every $q_i=a_i/b_i\ge0$ then each $a_i$ has the same sign as $b_i$ ($b_i>0$ by hypothesis), so every product $\prod_i a_i^{\alpha_i}\ge0$ and hence every summand in $N$ is $\ge0$. Thus $N\ge0$ for every representation, so every element of $S$ is a nonnegative rational number. Consequently no nonzero $s\in S$ can satisfy $-s\in S$. Therefore $(S,+)$ is additively reduced.

[b]II. $\mathbb{N}_0[q_1,\dots,q_n]$ additively reduced $\Rightarrow (q_1,\dots,q_n)\in\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}^n$[/b]

Assume $S=\mathbb{N}_0[q_1,\dots,q_n]$ is additively reduced and suppose, for contradiction, that some coordinate is negative. Without loss of generality let $q_j<0$. Write $q_j=\dfrac{a_j}{b_j}$ with $a_j\in\mathbb{Z}$, $b_j\in\mathbb{N}$; then $a_j<0$. Put $a:=-a_j>0$ so $q_j=-\dfrac{a}{b_j}$.

Consider the polynomial $F(x_j)=a+b_jx_j\in\mathbb{N}_0[x_j]\subset\mathbb{N}_0[x_1,\dots,x_n]$. Evaluating at the tuple gives $$ F(q_j)=a+b_j q_j=a+b_j\Big(-\frac{a}{b_j}\Big)=0. $$
Split $F$ as a sum of two nonzero polynomials with nonnegative coefficients: $$ F(x_j)=\big(a+(b_j-1)x_j\big)+x_j. $$
 Evaluate the two summands at the tuple; both evaluations lie in $S$ by definition: 
 $s:=\big(a+(b_j-1)q_j\big)\in S,\qquad t:=q_j\in S$ and $s+t=F(q)=0$. 
 
 Compute $s$ explicitly: $s=a+(b_j-1)\Big(-\frac{a}{b_j}\Big)=a-\frac{(b_j-1)a}{b_j}=\frac{a b_j-(b_j-1)a}{b_j}=\frac{a\big(b_j-(b_j-1)\big)}{b_j} = \frac{a}{b_j}>0$ so $s\neq 0$, while $t=q_j\neq 0$ by assumption. 
 Thus we have found nonzero $s,t\in S$ with $s+t=0$ contradicting the hypothesis that $S$ is additively reduced. Therefore no coordinate can be negative; every $q_i\ge0$.

Combining the two directions yields the claimed equivalence. $\square$
